docs.title: 人工智能和计算机开发基础
docs.text:
写给想真正理解 AI 与软件如何运转的读者。不预设背景，也不居高临下：不教写代码，也不教训模型，只求读完能判断：一条技术路线解决什么问题、 为什么有效、什么时候会失效。

全书两部分：

  • 人工智能基础：从神经元讲到智能体，含三条大模型架构路线的定性对照。
  • 计算机开发基础：从"程序是什么"讲到许可证政治，含可复现性与声明式系统。

docs.title: 读这本书
docs.text:
只想搞懂 AI 只想搞懂开发工具 想建立完整图景 第 1 部分 第 2 部分（2.1 起） 按顺序

docs.title: Three routes
docs.text:
What you want to sort out Where to read Roughly how many pages What artificial intelligence is actually about Part 1 150 Why the development toolchain looks the way it does Part 2 (from 2.1) 70 Build the complete picture The whole book, in order 230

Part 2 does not depend on Part 1. Part 1 does have internal dependencies: each section names its prerequisites at the start, and following that chain all the way back gives you all the background you need.

docs.title: The fixed structure of each section
docs.text:
Every section unfolds in the same six-beat rhythm:

  1. The one-line intuition — no jargon, just say the thing in plain words first.
  2. An everyday analogy — a scene you have lived through yourself.
  3. The diagram — look at the picture before the explanation.
  4. The problem it solves — why history needed this thing, and what happens without it.
  5. Its built-in limitations — the most important part of the section. Every weakness is derived from the principle, and the most common misconception gets named.
  6. Summary and self-check — three sentences of summary, two questions to test yourself.

A fixed structure has one side effect: on a second reading you can go through steps 1 and 5 only, and a whole book shrinks to two sheets of paper.

docs.title: On staying current
docs.text: Technical details go stale. The book's rule is: what will still hold in three years goes in the main text, what will not goes in a dated note box. So you will see qualifiers like "as of such-and-such a month" — those are not disclaimers, they are part of the information itself.

docs.title: On terminology
docs.text: The first time a term appears, the English original is given too, for example "gradient descent". This is not decoration: anyone who wants to look further needs to know what to search for.

docs.title: Preface
docs.text:
This book sets out to fix one specific kind of discomfort.

Open a browser today and you will run into the same handful of words: large model, compute, open source, parameters, agents. Each of them has an explanation somewhere, but nobody tells you how they relate to each other. So you end up in an awkward spot — you know these things are changing the world, yet you cannot say how the change is happening, still less which road leads into a wall.

That leaves two familiar kinds of book. One is popular science: you finish it knowing the story, but you still cannot judge anything. The other is a textbook: it asks you to work through three chapters of maths first. This book takes a third road. It does not teach you to calculate; it teaches you to judge. Every technical approach gets the same four questions — what is it trying to solve, why does it work, what does it cost, and when does it break.

The fourth question matters most, and it is the one most often left out. When a technology is introduced, its strengths are always crisp and its weaknesses blur into "there are still some limitations". This book does not accept that blur. Every weakness has to be derivable from the underlying principle, not copied from a news article.

The book has two parts. Part one covers artificial intelligence, from a single artificial neuron up to agents, and along the way sets the three main architecture families of large models side by side so you can see their trade-offs. Part two covers software development, from "what is a program" to licence politics, including version control, dependencies, reproducibility and declarative systems. You can read the two parts separately; together they make one complete picture, because the model is the most conspicuous layer of this system but not the only one.

Formulas do appear in the book, but only in the "Maths note" at the end of each section. Skip them and the main text still stands on its own; if you want to go deeper, they are there.

docs.title: Foundations of artificial intelligence
docs.text: This part starts from a single artificial neuron and ends at agents. Every section names its prerequisites; follow that chain back to the start and you are set.

docs.title: The one-line intuition
docs.text:
Artificial intelligence is not a product and not a technology: it is a goal — getting machines to do "the things that need intelligence". When that goal was written down in 1955 [1], the authors themselves could not say clearly what it covered. Seventy years on, its boundary is still moving.

This section does not try to define AI. Its job is to give you a map: from now on, whenever you hear a new word — large model, agent, deep learning — you can put it in the right place on that map and say how it relates to the layer next to it.

docs.title: An analogy: three generations of spam filtering
docs.text:
Think of one concrete task: deciding whether an email is spam.

First generation: people write the rules. "Block anything containing the word 'prize'." The machine only executes; all the intelligence sits in the head of the person writing the rules. Systems like this are still everywhere today, but their name is not AI, it is automation.

Second generation: the machine learns the rules. Give it ten thousand emails already labelled "spam / not spam" by humans and let it find the pattern itself. People no longer write rules; they supply two things only — the raw material (data) and the marking scheme (right or wrong). That is machine learning.

Third generation: the machine does the job itself. No labels at all; the machine discovers for itself that emails fall naturally into a few categories. Today's large language models mostly live on top of this layer — they do not just judge, they generate things that did not exist before.

The difference between these three generations is a difference in where the intelligence sits: in the first, in rules written by people; in the second, in parameters tuned from examples; in the third, in structure the machine finds for itself. Later chapters will come back to this ladder again and again.

docs.title: Four words, one map
docs.text:
Four words that the news mixes up freely are in fact nested inside one another (the figure below):

Artificial intelligence is the outermost goal. Machine learning is currently the main means of reaching it — tuning parameters from data. Deep learning is one branch of machine learning, using neural networks with many layers. Large language models are one product of deep learning. Almost everything called "AI" in the news today lives in the innermost ring; but the outer rings have not vanished — the robot arms in a factory, the route planning in a maps app, all of that is artificial intelligence too, just not the star of the news.

The point of the concentric circles is positioning. When you hear a new term, ask which layer it sits in, then ask how it relates to the neighbouring layer, and you will usually know which chapter's tools to reach for.

docs.title: Built-in limitations: the hard things are easy, the easy things are hard
docs.text:
The definition "the things that need intelligence" hides a trap: the word "intelligence" overrates the difficulty of some problems and underrates others.

Getting a machine to play Go beat the world champion back in 1997; getting a machine to cross a living room without hitting the furniture is still an open problem for the robotics industry. Getting a machine to recite the whole encyclopaedia is trivial; getting a machine to recognise the same cat in two photographs took decades to do properly. The psychologist Moravec summed up this contrast in one line: it is comparatively easy to make computers exhibit adult-level performance on intelligence tests or checkers, and difficult or impossible to give them the perceptual and mobility skills of a one-year-old [2].

The reason is not the machine, it is evolution: walking, recognising cats, hearing tone of voice are instincts polished over hundreds of millions of years. They feel effortless to us because evolution has hidden the computation behind them. Chess and arithmetic are only a few thousand years old; we have to work hard to learn them, and every rule sits out in the open — what sits out in the open, a machine can copy. This asymmetry is one of the base colours of the whole book: what a machine is good at never depends on how hard the task is for a person, but on whether the task's regularity can be expressed in data.

Common misconceptions

Thinking "AI is a thing", which is why questions like "when will AI take over the world" get asked. In reality AI is a set of goals whose boundary has been redrawn continuously for seventy years: today's AI and the AI of 1990 share only a name. A misconception of the same kind is "it can play chess, so it can think" — playing chess only shows that one particular datafied task is done well; see the green region in the figure above.

docs.title: Summary and self-check
docs.text:
Three sentences: AI is a goal, not a product; machine learning replaces "people write the rules" with "data plus a marking scheme"; and how strong a machine is does not follow how hard the task is for people, but whether the task's regularity can be expressed in data.

Two questions to check yourself:

  1. A meeting-scheduling system that "reads" emails and replies automatically — which generation does it belong to? And if its reading ability comes from a large language model?
  2. Why does "machines will never walk the way people do" need reassessing after the 2010s? (Hint: computation that evolution has hidden does not have to stay hidden forever.)

docs.title: The three schools of artificial intelligence
The one-line intuition
docs.text:
Under the goal of "making machines intelligent" sit three more fundamental questions: where does intelligence actually come from? In seventy years there have been three serious answers — from reasoning (symbolism), from connections (connectionism), from interaction (behaviourism). The winner in today's headlines is the second, but the other two are not dead; their blood still runs in the systems you use every day.

What this section gives you is not a history lesson but three pairs of glasses: take any AI system, and first ask which pair it sees the world through.

docs.title: An analogy: three paths up a mountain
docs.text:
One summit, three paths. Symbolism builds a cable car: every stretch of track has to be laid in advance by a person — safe, explainable, but where the track does not reach, you cannot go. Connectionism plants a vine: give it soil and climate (data) and the vine grows itself, at an astonishing rate, but nobody can say why each tendril bends the way it does. Behaviourism lets a goat loose: it climbs, it falls, it remembers which path works — nobody teaches it, but it really does arrive.

On all three paths someone has announced "this is the only real way up". The lesson of seventy years is that there is more than one summit, and not necessarily only one path.

docs.title: The problem it solves: three answers and their golden ages
docs.text:
Symbolism holds that intelligence is reasoning over symbols, so the core of an intelligent system is a clearly written knowledge base plus a set of inference rules. It gave birth to theorem proving, expert systems, and the earliest serious discussion of "can machines think" — in his 1950 paper Turing predicted that by the end of the century people would no longer argue about whether machines could think [3]. The claims made in its golden age later became its own burden: the rules can never be written completely, and even when they are, they cannot be maintained — this is the knowledge acquisition bottleneck, and the first-generation spam filter from section 1.1 is its miniature portrait.

Connectionism holds that intelligence is not in any single rule but in the way large numbers of simple units are connected. Its fortunes unfold in section 1.3 — two winters, two revivals, and today's leading large language models are its third-generation product.

Behaviourism holds that intelligence is not in the head but in the loop of "act, take the feedback, improve". Nobody hands it the right answer; the environment only says "good / bad", and the policy is accumulated by itself [4]. It runs from cybernetics all the way to robotics, never making headlines, never leaving the stage.

There is a pattern on the timeline in the figure above worth remembering: each school's strongest years are exactly the other two's weakest — funding, talent and patience move back and forth between the three, and the years when the move fails are called "AI winters". Textbooks organise them into three standard frameworks, divided by whether intelligence comes from reasoning, from learning, or from action [5], which line up one-to-one with the three schools here.

docs.title: Built-in limitations: each one's own wall
docs.text:
Each pair of glasses has somewhere it cannot see, and every wall grows out of that school's own assumptions:

For symbolism the wall is completeness: the world will not play by your rules, and the bigger the rule base, the more exceptions, until maintenance costs swallow all the gains. For connectionism the wall is transparency: the capability is stored in the weights, but nobody can read out "why it judged this way" — hard to fix when wrong, hard to explain when right. For behaviourism the wall is cost: trial and error means interacting with the world for real, a robot learning to walk has to take real falls, an agent learning to invest has to lose real money — not every environment allows you to try things at will.

The behaviourist loop (the figure above) is worth remembering on its own: action, feedback, improvement — nowhere on the ring is a "right answer" needed. This loop is the prototype of reinforcement learning in section 1.4, and it is also how the agents of section 1.7 improve themselves — the RSI stories are, at bottom, this loop wired into AI itself.

Common misconceptions

Thinking the three schools are historical relics and "only deep learning is left now". In reality today's winners are hybrids: the skeleton of a large language model is connectionist, much of the training that makes it "obedient" uses behaviourist feedback loops, and the part that calls a calendar or queries a database relies on precisely the old craft of symbolism — writing the world as a structure a machine can query. Do not throw away any of the three pairs of glasses.

docs.title: Summary and self-check
docs.text:
Three sentences: symbolism puts intelligence in clearly written rules, connectionism in the weights of connections, behaviourism in the loop with the environment; their walls are maintenance cost, opacity and the cost of trial and error; today's systems are a hybrid of all three.

Two questions to check yourself:

  1. For an app that "takes a photo of a plant and tells you whether you can eat it", what does each pair of glasses contribute?
  2. Why has the "knowledge acquisition bottleneck of expert systems" not disappeared with the arrival of large language models? (Hint: writing knowledge into rules and writing it into weights are different incarnations of the same difficulty.)

docs.title: Neural networks
docs.text: The notation in this section is used throughout the book. Before you start, remember three things: x is the input vector, w is the weights, f is the activation function. It's fine if that line means nothing yet — the prose doesn't need it.

docs.title: The one-line intuition
docs.text:
A human brain holds roughly eighty-six billion nerve cells[6], and each one does a single, extremely simple thing: it receives signals, and if they're strong enough it passes them on. No individual cell "understands" chess or reading, yet when they're wired together, those abilities appear. An artificial neuron copies that simple act exactly — and so, for the first time, something as complex as "intelligence" had a part you could compute with.

This section answers one question: how can a pile of parts that only do addition, subtraction and comparison produce anything useful.

docs.title: An analogy you use every day
docs.text:
Think about how a course decides pass or fail: final grade = coursework × 30% + exam × 70%, and 60 or above is a pass.

That rule already contains every part of an artificial neuron: two inputs (coursework, exam), two weights (30%, 70%), one weighted sum, one threshold (60), one output (1 for a pass, 0 for a fail). You don't decide who passes by memorising "which students passed" — you fix the weights and the threshold, and any new student's marks go in and the answer comes out on its own.

A perceptron does exactly the same thing, except the weights aren't set by a person — they're tuned from data.

Parts of the same colour do the same job: dendrites take signals in, the cell body integrates them, the axon sends them out; in an artificial neuron these three are called input, weighted sum and output. Note that the mapping is functional, not anatomical: what got borrowed is only the division of labour into receive, combine, send.

docs.title: The problem it solves
docs.text:
In 1943, McCulloch and Pitts proved something that looked impossible at the time: a logic unit that only does "weight, sum, threshold" can, once chained together, express any propositional logic[7]. That gave the idea that thought can be computed a concrete place to stand.

In 1958, Rosenblatt added one thing on top: the weights are not designed, they are tuned from examples[8]. That change is far bigger than it sounds. Before it, making a machine do a judgement task meant writing out every rule by hand — the symbolic approach, whose difficulties Section 1.2 described. The perceptron turned "do the task" into "tune the parameters": the rules moved out of human hands and into the data's.

So the word "learning" hasn't appeared yet in this section, but its stage is already set: as long as there is a way to tune weights automatically, judgement can grow out of experience. That way is called gradient descent, and it only takes the stage in Section 1.3.3.

docs.title: What one neuron can and cannot do
docs.text:
Give the two inputs of the figure above the values 0 or 1, and the judgements this neuron can make all share one geometric shape: draw a straight line on the plane; on one side the output is 1, on the other it's 0. This isn't a metaphor — the weighted sum is precisely the equation of a line. The weights set its direction, the threshold sets how far it sits from the origin.

Anything a straight line can separate, a single-layer perceptron can do. Anything it can't separate, it can't do at all. The most famous counterexample is XOR: same inputs give 0, different inputs give 1. Draw the four points on the plane (the figure below) and the two of each class always land on a diagonal, so any straight line must cut one of them over to the other side.

Circles sit at (0,0) and (1,1), triangles at (0,1) and (1,0): each class owns one diagonal. Of the three candidate cuts, the horizontal and vertical ones mix the classes half and half, and the diagonal one barely keeps a single triangle while shoving the other three to the far side — none of them survives.

In 1969, Minsky and Papert argued this thoroughly enough in Perceptrons[9], and since nobody then knew how to get past the wall, perceptron research stalled for nearly twenty years. Looking back, the way past it was almost flippant in its simplicity: add a few more neurons and fold straight lines into kinked ones. But "how do you get the stacked neurons to each tune their own weights" had no answer until backpropagation arrived — that's the subject of Section 1.3.3.

Remember one test now, because it comes back again and again: to judge a model, first ask what shape of boundary it can draw. The shape of the boundary decides which tasks it is naturally suited to, and that's the earliest source of "built-in strengths and weaknesses".

docs.title: A layer of interconnected neurons remembers a pattern
docs.text:
The last neuron was "pixels in, answer out". Now rearrange things: place nine neurons in a 3×3 grid, connected to each other, with no input layer and no output layer — each pixel position is itself a neuron, both an entrance and an exit.

How does a pattern get stored in the connections? There's one rule, fixed the moment you store it: two cells with the same colour in the pattern get connection weight +1; different colours get -1. Nine neurons, 36 connections, every weight computed straight from the pattern, no training at all — "set the pattern directly and let it remember", literally.

Memory works like this (the figure below): show the network a pattern with a piece missing, and each neuron multiplies every companion's current colour by the connection weight and adds them all up — positive total, it lights; negative, it stays dark. This happens on all nine neurons at once, one round, and the pattern refreshes once.

Do the arithmetic on the right half of the figure above: the "ten" that came in has had its centre erased, and the other eight pixels are correct. When it's the centre neuron's turn to vote, it counts its 8 companions — the 4 that shared its colour when the pattern was stored are now correctly lit and each contributes +1; the 4 that differed (the corners) are now correctly dark, and since different colour goes with negative weight, they also each contribute +1. Total +8, and the centre lights back up. Meanwhile each of the four arms computes +6 and stays lit, and each of the four corners computes -8 and stays dark — nobody gets dragged off course. One pixel wrong, one round of voting to fix it.

Networks like this are called associative memory today, and Hopfield proved in 1982 that this kind of voting always settles[10]. It's the simplest example of "a group of neurons directly remembers a pattern": the weight table is the memory, recall is the vote. And its built-in limitation is plain to see: this set of 36 weights knows exactly one pattern, "ten"; try to store an "X" as well and the two sets of weights fight — storing more means remembering more coarsely, and that's a tax every memory network pays.

docs.title: Summary and self-check
docs.text:
Three sentences: an artificial neuron = weighted sum of inputs + threshold; a single-layer perceptron's boundary is a straight line, so what it can and can't do follows from that shape; and a group of neurons can also store a pattern directly in its connection weights and recall it by voting — the weight table is the memory, but one net holds only one thing.

Two self-check questions:

  1. Change the threshold in the figure above from 60 to 90 — what happens to the decision boundary?
  2. A friend says: "The more neurons you have, the more problems a single-layer perceptron can solve." What's wrong with that?

Maths note. All the maths this section uses is the two lines below. Write the inputs as \(x_1, \dots, x_n\), the weights as \(w_1, \dots, w_n\), and the bias as \(b\) (which is just the negative of the threshold in the figure above):

Weighted sum:

\[z = \sum_{i=1}^{n} w_i x_i + b\]

Output (step activation):

\[y = \begin{cases} 1 & z \ge 0 \\ 0 & z < 0 \end{cases}\]

Connection weights and refresh rule for associative memory: when storing pattern \(s\), \(w_{ij} = +1\) if \(s_i = s_j\), otherwise \(-1\) (with \(w_{ii}=0\)); on recall each neuron computes \(h_i = \sum_{j \ne i} w_{ij}\, s_j\), and lights if \(h_i \ge 0\), stays dark if \(< 0\).

How weights get tuned from data (the learning rule) is collected in Section 1.3.3.

docs.title: Data input: from real quantities to high-dimensional vectors
The one-line intuition
docs.text:
The neuron from Section 1.3.1 does one thing: it takes numbers and computes a weighted sum. It doesn't know red, it doesn't know Chinese characters, it doesn't know cats. So everything in the world — photos, speech, text, the way you're walking right now — has to settle one thing first before it can enter a neural network: it has to become a column of numbers.

This section is about the craft of that transformation. Once it's done, a thing is represented by its column of numbers, and however many cells that column has, we say the world has that many dimensions.

docs.title: An analogy: a medical report
docs.text:
A medical report compresses "you as a person" into a few hundred numbers: height, weight, blood pressure, twenty blood markers… The doctor has never met you, but reading the numbers alone lets them make a reasonably reliable judgement. Compression necessarily loses things — your personality isn't in the report — but if the markers are chosen well, what gets lost is exactly the part that doesn't affect the judgement.

That's the kind of report a neural network eats. Choose its "tests" well and it learns fast and accurately; choose them badly and no amount of genius will save it.

docs.title: Images: from colour to tensor
docs.text:
A digital photo is, on screen, already an array of numbers: three numbers per pixel, describing the intensity of red, green and blue light (0 to 255). So "feeding a photo to the network" isn't translation, it's copying — except you're copying three million numbers (the figure below).

Greyscale is simpler: black-and-white handwritten digits are usually made into a 28×28 grid, each cell a number from 0 to 1. Straighten the 784 cells out row by row and you get a 784-dimensional vector (the figure below) — 784 is the "dimensionality" this world hands the network.

Straightening loses no information but it does lose relationships: two pixels that sat next to each other on the paper are 28 positions apart in the vector, and the network has to relearn "next to each other" for itself. That's the starting point for a lot of later architecture inventions — file it away for now.

docs.title: Text: from characters to chunks
docs.text:
Numbers and images are numbers by nature. Text isn't, so it has to be cut up first. The cutting method is a purely engineering trade-off (the figure below); the mainstream approach is called BPE (byte-pair encoding)[11]: start from single characters, repeatedly count which pair of partners occurs most often in the corpus, and merge them into a new symbol. After tens of thousands of rounds, common words have been merged into whole chunks and rare words have fallen back to characters — one vocabulary serving both ends.

Each chunk that comes out is called a token. The model's eyes see no words, only tokens and their ids. Chinese has no spaces and its characters are all common, so BPE usually doesn't merge Chinese characters, and the same passage costs two or three times as many tokens in Chinese as in English — a ratio that turns into a hard cash constraint when we get to the context window in Section 1.5.

docs.title: Where the data comes from
docs.text:
Vectors are the "shape"; data is the "material". The material has three sources: naturally labelled (the star rating when you order takeaway, the timestamp on a photo), labelled with money and labour (medical images need a doctor to draw the boxes), and self-generated (take text off the internet directly — "the next sentence" is a free ground truth, which is the single most important insight of the large language model era; Section 1.5 expands on it).

Dirty data makes a dirty model: an annotator's hand slips, a crawler drags in duplicate samples, a form gets one cell copied wrong — the network faithfully learns those errors too, and learns them just as eagerly.

docs.title: Built-in limitations: dimension is a choice, and choices cost
docs.text:
Turning the world into vectors means making a decision at every step: using 784 cells to represent a digit is deciding "ignore stroke thickness and colour"; using three numbers for a pixel is deciding "the way hue and brightness combine doesn't matter". Whatever the representation throws away, the network can never learn back.

The subtler cost is dimension itself: the higher it goes, the less "nearby" means anything — in a 784-dimensional space two points are neither far nor close. The curse of dimensionality, put plainly, is this: the more cells there are, the more samples you need, or most cells will wait their whole lives for a single example.

Common misconceptions

That "AI sees" the photo. It doesn't. It reads a numerical spreadsheet whose format — dimensions, order, the value range of each cell — was all decided by people; two worlds with different formats are two different worlds to it. That's also why "show the AI what a human eye sees" always has a layer of representation in between — and the biases in that representation pass straight through to the model.

docs.title: Summary and self-check
docs.text:
Three sentences: every input first becomes a fixed-length vector, and the dimensionality is just "how many numbers it took to describe a thing"; text gets cut into tokens, and vocabulary size is the dividing line between "how much to memorise" and "how much to assemble"; what the representation throws away can never be learned back, and dirty data gets learned just as eagerly.

Two self-check questions:

  1. Rotate a 28×28 handwritten digit by 90 degrees and then straighten it — does the resulting vector have any relationship to the original? What does that say about the flattening representation?
  2. An app needs to recognise handwritten Chinese characters. Should its vocabulary lean large or small? (Hint: whether Chinese characters are "characters" or "chunks" depends on whether you want the model to memorise or to assemble.)

Maths note. This section only introduces notation: the input vector is written in bold as \(\mathbf{x} = (x_1, x_2, \dots, x_d)\), where \(d\) is the dimensionality; the array formed by stacking an image's three colour layers is called a tensor, which is just the mathematical name for "a multi-dimensional table". The BPE merging rule involves no maths, only counting.

docs.title: Finding patterns in high dimensions: how a neural network learns
The one-line intuition
docs.text:
Learning is turning knobs: a network holds anywhere from a few million to a few hundred billion parameters (Section 1.3.1 counted them), each one a knob. At the start of training they're all turned at random and the network talks nonsense; then you do the same thing over and over — look at a batch of examples, measure how badly it's getting things wrong, and nudge every knob a little way towards "less wrong". A few million rounds later, the combination of knob positions starts producing correct answers.

No inspiration, no epiphany, just those two moves — measure the error, turn the knobs — repeated a few million times.

docs.title: An analogy: tuning blindfolded
docs.text:
Imagine tuning an old radio with two hundred knobs while blindfolded, with the goal of hearing a clean jazz station. You can't see the knobs, but you can hear how loud the static is. There's only one strategy: nudge each knob a little, listen to whether the static got louder or quieter, and keep turning in whichever direction made it quieter. Two hundred knobs in turn, and after a few dozen rounds the music surfaces.

"Hearing whether the static went up or down" is the loss function; "turning towards less static" is gradient descent. The only difference is that a neural network's two hundred knobs affect each other, and there are tens of billions of them.

docs.title: The problem it solves
docs.text: Section 1.3.1 left two loose ends: the XOR wall gets climbed by "adding a few more neurons", but nobody knew how to get each one to tune its own weights. This section is the answer.

docs.title: Start with the simplest case: two neurons, one kinked line
docs.text:
The cheapest way into "learning" is a "mini network" with only four weights: give it a pile of orange data points and ask it to draw the line through them (Figure 1-15).

There are only two neurons in it. Section 1.3.1 said each neuron does two things: first compute a straight line (the weighted sum), then pass the result through a nonlinearity. The most common one is astonishingly plain — flatten negatives to zero: any negative number becomes 0, positive numbers pass through unchanged. Its only effect is to "fold" the line at zero, creating a kink.

And so it fits together: each neuron contributes one kink. Two neurons, two kinks, and together they make a V-shaped line assembled from two straight segments — in Figure 1-15 the two coloured kinked lines add up to the blue V, and the orange data points sit on it. Take it to ten neurons and you have ten kinks; take it to a few hundred and the kinks are too dense to see, and the line can hug any curve at all.

This is the smallest version of "finding patterns in high dimensions": the pattern is that line — it passes through every point it was taught, and its kinks imitate every bend in the data. A real network scales the game up by a billion: the input is a 784-dimensional vector, the "line" is a folded surface in thirty-million-dimensional space, but "each neuron folds once, and the sum assembles a complex mapping" needs not one word changed.

And while we're here, see its limit plainly: no matter how many kinks, it's only imitating the trend from point to point. It's a parrot, imitating the patterns it has seen beautifully and knowing nothing beyond them — and that parrot comes back in Section 1.6 (the seed of hallucination gets planted right here).

The key moves come in three steps, each with a figure.

Step one: give "badly wrong" a number. The network takes a training example, computes a prediction, subtracts it from the ground truth, squares, averages — and gets a single number, the loss. Big loss = badly wrong; small loss = close to correct. All of training is about making that number smaller.

Step two: find downhill in "knob space". Treat every parameter as an axis, and the loss becomes the height of that high-dimensional space — together, a rolling surface (the figure below draws a miniature of it with two parameters). The rule of gradient descent is one plain sentence: work out the steepest downhill direction from where you are, take a small step that way, repeat. The size of that "small step" is the learning rate — too big and you leap clean over the valley floor and bounce back and forth, too small and you'll never get there in a hundred years.

Step three: work out which way each knob should turn. With tens of millions of parameters on the surface, how do you know the "steepest downhill"? That's the gift of backpropagation in 1986[12]: first compute the prediction forwards (grey line), then start from the error at the output layer and split the bill layer by layer from right to left (red line) — each weight is told "how much of this error is your responsibility", and the ones with more responsibility get turned further, the ones with less get turned less (the figure below). One chain rule, and the direction for tens of billions of knobs is worked out in a single pass.

One run through all three steps is called an iteration. After a few billion iterations, the little 26-knob network from Section 1.3.1 classifies correctly, and the same mechanism scaled up ten thousandfold is what LeCun and colleagues had in their earliest convolutional networks[13] and what underlies every large model today.

docs.title: Finding patterns in high dimensions: the data lives on a sheet of paper
docs.text:
One puzzle is left: thirty-million-dimensional space is so empty, how could a few hundred cat photos teach a network to recognise cats?

Because data doesn't fill the space. All the ways one "photo of a cat" differs from another — angle, lighting, distance, pose — have only a handful of degrees of freedom, so in thirty-million-dimensional space they cluster on a curved, low-dimensional sheet, and that sheet is called a manifold[14]. Learning is getting to know the shape of that sheet: unroll the curled-up parts, pull the same class together and push different classes apart (the figure below).

That also explains why "high-dimensional" isn't as scary as it sounds: dimension is the raw material of representation; the pattern lives on a low-dimensional manifold. How well a network learns depends on whether it can follow the sheet the data actually sits on, rather than being led astray into the empty regions of the space.

docs.title: Built-in limitations: gradient descent only guarantees "better", not "right"
docs.text:
Downhill on that surface has three kinds of pit. Local pits: land in a small dip and everything around is uphill, so the robot thinks it has hit the valley floor — luckily, real local minima in high dimensions are far rarer than two-dimensional intuition suggests. Overfitting: learning the training data off by heart, loss falling all the way, then falling apart on a new example — how to spot and prevent that is the star of Section 1.4.3. Data hunger: the more parameters, the more examples you have to feed it, or the knobs memorise each sample instead of the pattern.

Common misconceptions

That a neural network "learns like a brain". Real training is a numerical optimisation machine: loss function, gradient, update, every step deterministic arithmetic. The brain gives it only the inspiration (the three-step structure of Section 1.3.1); the learning itself is entirely engineering. By the same token, "the network figured it out" has no counterpart either — it's just that after some iteration, the loss happened to drop to a particular place.

docs.title: Summary and self-check
docs.text:
Three sentences: the loss function turns "badly wrong" into a number; gradient descent turns the knobs along the steepest downhill; backpropagation splits the error bill back to every weight across the network. Learning has no flash of insight, only a few million rounds of "measure the error, turn the knobs" — and a trained network is essentially a parrot: imitating the patterns it has seen beautifully.

Two self-check questions:

  1. What happens if you set the learning rate ten times higher? And a tenth of that? (Hint: imagine the step size on the figure above.)
  2. Why can "a few dozen cat photos" teach a model to recognise cats, while "a few dozen calculus problems" can't teach a model calculus? (Hint: manifolds.)

Maths note. Write the prediction as \(\hat{y}\) and the ground truth as \(y\); the mean squared error loss is:

\[L = rac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n} (\hat{y}_i - y_i)^2\]

The "fold" of each neuron is just \(h = \max(0,\, wx+b)\) ("flatten negatives to zero"), after which the various \(h\) are summed with weights.

The gradient descent update is: \( heta \leftarrow heta - \eta abla L\), where \( heta\) is all the parameters, \(\eta\) is the learning rate, and \( abla L\) is the gradient of the loss with respect to each parameter (the "steepest downhill direction"). Backpropagation is simply using the chain rule to compute every component of \( abla L\) in one pass.

docs.title: Learning it and using it: training and inference
The one-line intuition
docs.text:
The "measure the error, turn the knobs" of Section 1.3.3 is training; once training ends and the knobs are frozen, giving the network a new question and having it compute forwards once for an answer is inference. One network, two lives: in training it changes, in inference it doesn't.

Separating these two is the precondition for understanding large-model cost, speed, and every question of the form "did it actually learn that".

docs.title: An analogy: developing the recipe vs serving from it
docs.text:
New dish development at a restaurant chain is training: taste, take feedback, change the recipe, revise it dozens of times, with the best chefs and the most expensive ingredients, and weeks to finalise one dish. Serving from that recipe in every branch is inference: the recipe (the weights) is frozen, each plate is just execution, minutes apiece, millions of covers.

The key is where the line falls: the moment the recipe is fixed. After that, no matter how popular a branch's output is, the recipe doesn't change itself — unless head office decides on a new version, and that's a fresh round of training.

docs.title: Two phases, two cost structures
docs.text:
Training computes both forwards and backwards: forwards gives the prediction, backwards splits the bill and turns the knobs (Section 1.3.3). It has to swallow vast amounts of data, run for weeks, burn the electricity of a whole machine room — but it happens only once in its life (strictly: once per model version).

Inference is forwards only: a question comes in, the signal passes left to right through the network, an answer comes out. No error, no gradient, no knob moves. A single inference takes milliseconds, but the world runs billions of them every day — a cheap unit price times an astronomical count is the real cost structure of a large-model company.

That's also why "what does one training run cost" and "what does one question cost" are two completely different quotes in the industry: the first is R&D, the second is a branch's ingredients and utilities.

docs.title: What lives in video memory during inference
docs.text:
Inference computes less, but the network weights must live in video memory in their entirety, plus room for the computation in progress and the conversation history (the figure below). That's the first of the "video memory walls" deployers go on about: whether a model can run at all depends on whether the wall is tall enough.

Two threads get planted here, each with a section to pick it up later: why the conversation-history cache "grows and grows", which leads to the structure of attention (Section 1.5.2) and the KV cache (Section 1.8); and "what if the wall is too tall", which leads to quantization and precision (Section 1.8).

docs.title: Built-in limitations: once it's fixed, it learns nothing more from you
docs.text:
During inference, nothing you say and nothing you correct moves a single weight. Spend an afternoon arguing the model into silence, close the window, and next time it makes the same mistake — there is no such thing as "remembering this lesson" (to really change it you have to go back to the training side, which is called fine-tuning or alignment, Section 1.6).

Common misconceptions

That "the AI is learning while it chats with me". Almost all of what users experience as "it understands me better now" comes from the preceding text it can see in the conversation window (the context, Section 1.7.1), not from weights changing. Keep those two apart and a lot of confusion — "why has it forgotten everything in a new session", "why can't it learn my preferences" — disappears at once.

docs.title: Summary and self-check
docs.text:
Three sentences: training computes forwards and backwards, the knobs move, and it happens once in a lifetime; inference computes forwards only, the knobs are frozen, and it happens billions of times a day; the video memory wall first constrains "will it fit", then "how long can we chat".

Two self-check questions:

  1. A product claims "the more you chat with it, the better it understands you". Using this section's framework, list the two things you'd need to confirm to verify that claim.
  2. A restaurant outsources "new dish development" to three branches to each try recipes. Describe the problem with that in the language of training and inference.

docs.title: Machine learning
docs.text:
This chapter scales "learning" up from a single neuron to a whole discipline: first where depth comes from (how stacking layers taught a network to bend), then the three learning paradigms — learning against the answer key, finding structure on your own, and trial and error against the world; and finally the most practical question of all: how do you tell whether it has actually learned anything?

The three sections stand fairly independent; Section 1.4.3 also works as a standalone read — it skips the theory and talks only about how to sign off.

docs.title: A deeper brain: multilayer perceptrons and deep learning
The one-line intuition
docs.text: The single-layer perceptron of Section 1.3.1 can only draw one straight line; Section 1.3.3 showed how to turn the knobs, but no matter how many knobs there are, a one-layer network still draws straight lines. Put a layer between the input and the output and the straight line learns to bend — that layer is called the hidden layer, and with it the new era finally has something to attach the word "depth" to.

docs.title: An analogy: answer the small questions first
docs.text:
Faced with "is this face a cat", nobody stares at pixels and concludes directly. You run a string of small questions in your head: does it have ears? Are the ears pointed? Is there a whisker? Each small question is one neuron, and their answers are pooled by a last neuron that draws the big conclusion.

Answer the small questions, then answer the big one with those answers — that is all a multilayer network does. Those "small-question neurons" sit between input and output, invisible and untouchable, which is why they are called the hidden layer.

docs.title: The problem it solves: which space the line is drawn in
docs.text:
First, cash in the question Section 1.3.3 left hanging: how does a multilayer network get through XOR?

The trick is a straight line in high dimensions, a projection in low ones. The hidden layer sends every input into a new coordinate system: each dimension is one hidden neuron's yes/no answer. In that new space the boundary the network draws is a flat hyperplane — a straight line in a high-dimensional space; project the same surface back onto the familiar 2-D plane and it becomes a bent line, a band, or a boundary so complicated you cannot name its shape at first glance (Figure 1-21).

One line, straight up high and complicated down low — that is the entire secret of how an MLP solves XOR.

Projected back onto the original plane, that straight line shows its true face: a hyperbola, its two branches cutting the corners of the two circles — triangles on one side of the curve, circles on the other. Beating the XOR wall works exactly like this: it is not that one line learned to bend, but that a straight line in high dimensions can project down as a complicated curve.

The "deep" in "deep learning" is the number of hidden layers. One layer is the post-1986 MLP; a dozen layers, a few hundred layers, is the deep network that took over the field after 2012 [15]. Why is stacking layers worth it? Compositional reuse: the small parts the first layer learns (edges, corners) are picked up directly by the second layer to build bigger parts (ears, whiskers), and the third assembles a whole cat — no part has to be learned twice. A flat, wide network needs far more parameters to express the same thing [16].

While we are here, one missing piece: in the curve-fitting mini-network of Section 1.3.3, the neurons passed their output straight through. In a real network every neuron goes through a nonlinear activation (say, "anything negative becomes zero"), because otherwise however many layers you stack, the whole pile collapses mathematically into a single straight line — nonlinearity is what makes "depth" mean anything, and it is the shared source of both the power of deep networks and their opacity [17].

docs.title: Built-in limitations: three bills
docs.text:
The power of a deep network is bought with three things. Data: hundreds of millions of parameters means examples on the same scale, or you overfit (Section 1.4.3). Compute: millions of forward-and-backward passes, each one touching the whole network — this is why deep learning slept until 2012, and what woke it was not a new theory but graphics cards. Transparency: the deeper the stack, the harder it is to answer "why did it decide that", and even the people who built it cannot say.

Common misconceptions

People assume "deep = smarter", that capability grows automatically as you add layers. Layers only supply expressive potential — the ability to draw more complicated boundaries; turning that potential into capability takes data and compute, and takes good training to realise. A very deep network with very little data losing to a shallow network with plenty of data is the norm, not news.

docs.title: Summary and self-check
docs.text:
In three sentences: the hidden layer lets the network build a new space in which straight lines are enough, and a bent line in the old space is straight in the new one; stack hidden layers and you have deep learning, whose power comes from reusing parts compositionally; the price is three bills — data, compute and transparency.

Two self-check questions:

  1. Draw the straight line from the right panel of Figure 1-20 into the input space of the left panel — what shape does it take?
  2. Why can a single neuron also draw a curved line if you feed it an x² among its inputs (the mini-network of Section 1.3.3)? What does that have in common with what a hidden layer does?

Maths note. Every hidden neuron: \(h_j = f(\sum_i w_{ij} x_i + b_j)\), where \(f\) is a nonlinear activation (\(f(z)=\max(0,z)\), say, negatives to zero). A multilayer network is this expression nested over several layers. "Without \(f\), depth collapses into one layer" takes one line to verify: composing two linear layers is still a linear map.

docs.title: The one-line intuition
docs.text:
Three learning paradigms, and the only difference is what signal you are holding while learning: supervised learning has the answer key, unsupervised learning has only the data itself, and reinforcement learning has a single score — usually one handed over long after the fact.

The same problem asked three ways produces three completely different products and three different bills. If you can recognise which way is being asked, you can predict where it will be expensive and where it will fall over.

docs.title: An analogy: three students learning to cook
docs.text:
The supervised student has a master chef standing alongside, tasting every dish the moment it is finished: "too much salt", "heat's too high". The feedback is dense, specific and repeatable — but the chef's tongue is expensive, and every dish needs someone to taste it.

The unsupervised student has no teacher, only a fridge full of ingredients, and sorts them by similarity: these have gone mouldy, these will keep a week. Nobody tells them whether the sorting is right; they might sort by origin, or by colour — it can separate them, but the separation need not mean anything.

The reinforcement student is an apprentice in a real restaurant: nobody says what was wrong with each dish, only the boss's remark at month end — "not bad this month". The score arrives late, arrives rarely, and the student has to guess which step (which dish) earned it.

docs.title: Supervised learning: learning with the answers
docs.text:
Ten thousand emails, each labelled "spam" or "normal", and the model learns to tell them apart — the spam filter of Section 1.1 is exactly this. Classification, regression, translation, speech recognition: all of them are doing the same thing underneath, finding a mapping from input to answer given pairs of (input, answer).

The cost is direct: somebody has to supply the answers. Medical images need a doctor to draw the boxes, legal documents need a lawyer to mark the clauses, dialect audio needs someone who speaks the dialect to transcribe it — the price of labelling often exceeds the price of training. The weakness is just as direct: it is reliable only within "the kinds of answer that have appeared before"; meet something absent from the training set and it forces the new thing into an old answer.

docs.title: Unsupervised learning, and its most successful branch
docs.text:
This branch has no answers, so the machine has to find structure for itself: group similar things together (clustering), squash high dimensions into a few you can plot (dimensionality reduction), pick out the odd ones (anomaly detection). The manifold of Section 1.3.3 is exactly this in action — working out which sheet of paper the data lives on.

Its soft spot is that there is no referee: you get ten clusters, and are they "problem types" or "greeting lengths"? Nobody can count their way to an answer. Evaluation is hard, so it tends to be used as an exploration tool rather than a finished product on the production line.

But one of its branches went on to upend the whole industry. Self-supervision: split the data itself into "question" and "answer" — take a passage, mask the last word, have the model guess it; then check against the answer, which is the original text. No labelling cost, and a near-infinite supply of practice questions. Strictly it belongs to the unsupervised family, but it is far more powerful than the rest of it — large language models were raised on it, and Section 1.5 is about nothing else.

docs.title: Reinforcement learning: learning from a score alone
docs.text:
Playing chess, teaching a robot to walk, scheduling jobs across a data centre — none of these has an answer key, only how the ending went: win or lose, fall or stand, power bill high or low.

The difficulty is not in the "learning", it is in attribution [18]: a game runs a hundred-plus moves, you win, so how much credit belongs to move 3 and how much to move 97? The score arrives once, at the very end, and usually very sparsely (Figure 1-18) — this is the credit assignment problem. Spreading the score backwards across every step is the same kind of mental work as backpropagation spreading the error back across every weight in Section 1.3.3.

The second trap in reinforcement learning is that trial and error costs real money: a robot learning to walk takes real falls, a recommender learning what to show offends real users. So real systems usually practise in a simulated environment first and fine-tune once live — and if the simulation is unlike reality, the skill does not transfer.

docs.title: Built-in limitations: three signals, three kinds of damage
docs.text:
Supervision's damage is in coverage: it does not know the world beyond its answers. Unsupervised learning's damage is in the referee: the structure it finds need not mean anything, and is hard to verify. Reinforcement learning's damage is in attribution and cost: late sparse scores are hard to spread, and trial and error in a real environment burns money.

One practical test: look at how it fails and you know which branch it is. Wrong but "wrong with great confidence" is usually coverage (supervised); results that "look structured but are useless" are usually the referee (unsupervised); "great at gaming the score, useless at the job" is usually attribution (reinforcement).

Common misconceptions

People assume "unsupervised" means "nobody is in charge, it just learns whatever". Its precise meaning is "no answer key", and its success often depends on people more, not less — how the data is prepared, how the structure is interpreted, how the result is evaluated are all human work. Another common mistake is treating self-supervision as a fourth paradigm: it belongs to the unsupervised family, and "questions and answers both grown from the data" is its technique, not its category.

docs.title: Summary and self-check
docs.text:
In three sentences: the three paradigms differ only in the learning signal — answers, data alone, a score alone; the core difficulty of reinforcement learning is credit assignment and the cost of trial and error; unsupervised learning has no referee, and its most successful branch, self-supervision, is what feeds every large model.

Two self-check questions:

  1. A system that "predicts tomorrow's electricity price from historical demand curves" — which paradigm is it most likely to use? Where does its labelling cost sit?
  2. Why can "process rewards" speed up reinforcement learning and yet also teach it bad habits? (Hint: the "gaming the score" in Figure 1-18.)

docs.title: Has it actually learned? Generalization, overfitting and evaluation
The one-line intuition
docs.text:
A model that performs well on its training data has told you almost nothing. The real skill is generalizing — still performing well on data it has never seen. This section is about how to know it has managed that, and how it pretends to have.

This is the second turning point in the book. So far we have discussed "how it learns"; from here on we discuss "how you know it has learned" — and that second question is the line between treating AI as engineering and treating it as a faith.

docs.title: An analogy: memorising the workbook versus solving the paper
docs.text:
Two students both score 95 on the same paper. One understood the method and scores 90 on a fresh paper; the other memorised every answer in the workbook and fails outright on a fresh paper.

Same score, different skill. Models are the same: if the "kinks" of Section 1.3.3 simply pass exactly through every training point, what it learned is not the pattern, it is this workbook (Figure 1-19).

docs.title: Three ways of "learning"
docs.text:
Underfitting: it has not even learned the training data, and misses the trend — too few kinks, too few parameters.

Overfitting: it knows the training data inside out, noise included, and draws wobbles that do not exist in the data — too many parameters, trained too long.

Just right: it catches the trend and tolerates the odd deviation. There is no natural boundary between the three, only a continuous spectrum from "fitting a bit more" to "memorising a bit more".

Curiously, look at the three training scores: underfitting is lowest, just right is in the middle, overfitting scores 100. Training score and real skill run in opposite directions on the overfitting side — which is why "just watch the training loss" tells you nothing.

docs.title: What to examine it with
docs.text:
So hold data back as an exam paper. Ten thousand records split three ways (Figure 1-20): the training set adjusts the weights; the validation set picks the model, sets the hyperparameters and decides when to stop; the test set is sat exactly once, at the end.

Validation and test sets are both "data it has not seen"; the difference is what you do with it, and how many times you use it.

The validation set is a mock exam: you can review the paper afterwards, you can sit it again and again — you use its score to pick the model, tune the learning rate, decide when to stop. It is part of your decision loop. The test set is the final exam: sat once, after everything is fixed, and its score goes into what you promise the outside world.

Why can the test set only be sat once, when it is "just inference mode"? The model genuinely does not learn at inference time, but you do: every time you look at a test score you make a decision from it — pick this version, run another round, change the architecture. Decision information leaks back to the training side through your hands. The more times you sit it, the more leaks, and the more the score resembles a validation score rather than a final exam. Hence the engineering rule: a test score is read once, fixed once, and then left alone.

docs.title: The most useful diagnostic: two loss curves
docs.text: Training loss falls all the way down; validation loss falls and then rises — at the moment it turns up, the model has started memorising the workbook (Figure 1-21). That fork is the most important reading in training: stop too early and you underfit, stop too late and you overfit, and "when to stop" is itself a decision (known in engineering as early stopping).

docs.title: Why evaluation lies
docs.text:
Even with the process perfectly correct, the numbers are often dishonest. Three of the commonest cheats (Figure 1-22):

Data leakage — exam questions got into the question bank. Randomly splitting a time series (using the future to predict the past), two scans of the same patient landing on opposite sides of the split, the answer hiding in the inputs (predicting "will this be refunded" while using "refund amount" as a feature). The symptom is always the same: offline scores that are suspiciously high.

Distribution shift — the paper and the era moved on. A model scoring 95 on last year's data quietly slides to 70 as this year's users change habits; if the evaluation set is never refreshed, the metric becomes a placebo.

The metric itself being gamed — this is Goodhart's law: once a measure becomes a target, it stops being a good measure. Models that grind the leaderboard, models that write answers in the style of the evaluation set, are footnotes to that law [19].

docs.title: Built-in limitations: a guarantee of generalization does not exist
docs.text:
Geometrically you can think of it like this: the model "draws lines" between training points, and however smoothly it draws them, they are still only guesses; the real pattern may bend somewhere you hold no data. The manifold hypothesis (Section 1.3.3) tells us the data lives on a low-dimensional sheet, but nobody guarantees that sheet stays smooth where you did not sample.

In other words: generalization is induction, and induction always needs assumptions. All evaluation can do is expose where the assumptions fail; it cannot remove them. This is the bedrock of every discussion about "interpretability" and "trustworthy AI", and one of the roots of the hallucination problem in Section 1.6.

Common misconceptions

People assume "99% accuracy" means a good model. Under class imbalance, 99% may just be another way of saying "it gets every single minority case wrong" (with 990 of 1,000 samples being normal email, always answering "normal" is 99%). So before reading any metric, ask three things: how are the classes distributed, where did the test set come from, and how many times has this score been tuned?

docs.title: Summary and self-check
docs.text:
In three sentences: a training score says nothing about skill, only unseen data does; overfitting is memorising the workbook, and there training score and real skill run in opposite directions; evaluation is fooled by leakage, drift and gameable metrics — a guarantee of generalization does not exist, so design can only expose failure.

Two self-check questions:

  1. A model scores 99% on the training set, 62% on validation and 61% on test. Is the problem the model or the process? What do you look at first?
  2. Why is "random splitting" itself a form of data leakage in tasks like predicting share prices or disease risk?

Maths note. Write the training loss as \(L_{\text{train}}\) and the validation loss as \(L_{\text{val}}\). In the overfitting region \(L_{\text{train}}\) keeps falling while \(L_{\text{val}}\) rises; early stopping takes the minimum of \(L_{\text{val}}\). Generalization error decomposes roughly as \(L_{\text{val}} \approx \text{bias}^2 + \text{variance} + \text{noise}\): underfitting is high bias, overfitting is high variance, and just right is the compromise [20].

docs.title: Large language models
docs.text: This chapter first lays out the premise shared by all three architectural routes: what large models do, how multimodality joins in, and why scale works (the first three sections); then we take the routes one by one. The reading order is the dependency order: skip the scaling laws and go straight to attention, and "why build them this big" won't make sense.

docs.title: Start with the simplest case: all it does is predict the next word
docs.text:
Strip away all the product packaging, and a large language model does exactly one thing in training: give it some text, and it guesses what the next token is (Figure 1-23). Then it checks the answer, and the answer is the original text — this is the self-supervision described in Section 1.4.2, with an endless supply of practice questions.

"It only guesses the next word" sounds unworthy of the word "intelligence". But to get the next word right, the model is forced to learn a great deal: predicting "sky" after "the" means knowing collocations, predicting 3288 after "137×24=" means doing arithmetic, predicting the title after "Jane Austen's best-known novel is" means remembering facts. The prediction objective forces the model to compress every regularity in language into its parameters. The abilities it shows are a by-product; the objective is always prediction. Models of this kind — self-supervised pretraining on enormous data, then adapted to all sorts of tasks — are collectively called foundation models [21].

docs.title: Multimodal: different senses, one representation space
docs.text: Beyond text, images are cut into little tiles and audio into short frames, each passing through an encoder and all mapped into the same representation space (in Figure 1-21 we saw "everything is a column of numbers"; this is the multi-sensory version). The point isn't "it can read images" but alignment: during training, paired "image and its textual description" are pulled together in that space, so the model learns that both maps share one set of place names [22][23].

docs.title: One forward pass, one character grown
docs.text: The full inference loop (Figure 1-23) is worth another look: input is cut into tokens → passes through dozens of layers → out comes a probability table for the next token → one is drawn by some strategy → it is stuck on the end of the sentence → go again. The long answer you read is this diagram looping hundreds of times, each time growing a single character.

docs.title: Built-in limitations: predicting the next word doesn't judge truth
docs.text:
There is no "true" dimension in the training objective — the training data is the internet, and the internet holds both errors and truths, which the model learns from indiscriminately as "what usually comes next". Fluency and truth were never distinguished in the training objective; that is the mechanistic source of hallucination, expanded in Section 1.6.

Common misconceptions

The belief that "it checks before answering". By default it does no retrieval or verification at all — the probability table comes from regularities compressed into its parameters, not from a database. Products that do verify have wrapped retrieval around the outside, as described in Section 1.7.3.

docs.title: Qualitative tiers (as of the second half of 2026)
docs.text:
Capability tiers (qualitative, as of late 2026)

First tier (leading on general capability and ecosystem): GPT, Claude, Gemini, DeepSeek. Second tier (open-source and regional leaders): Llama, Mistral, Qwen, Gemma and others.

Tiers only reflect "roughly where things sit on mainstream benchmarks and public experience"; no scores, no ranking. Places change by the month, so go by current public evaluations when you read this book.

docs.title: Summary and self-check
docs.text:
Three sentences: a large model does one thing, predict the next token; multimodality uses alignment to feed different senses into one representation space; fluency and truth were never distinguished in the training objective.

Two self-check questions:

  1. Why is "self-supervision" decisive for this field? (Hint: think about the price of labels.)
  2. A model needs hundreds of forward passes to finish one sentence, so what is the most direct way to "cut inference cost"?

docs.title: The one-line intuition
docs.text: In this field, "bigger" is not a mystical slogan but a curve you can draw in advance: make the model bigger (parameters, data and compute all growing together) and the loss falls along a smooth power law, with the amount of the fall predictable before training starts. This curve is the scaling law, and it is the ledger that lets the whole industry stake billions on it.

docs.title: An analogy: economies of scale
docs.text: Double a factory's output and unit cost falls by a fixed proportion — that is economies of scale in industry. Large models moved this onto "intelligence": each time inputs (compute, data, parameters) multiply, the loss falls by a fixed proportion, and that proportion can be predicted in advance [24]. It is not "bigger might be better" but "bigger is necessarily better along a curve" — and that curve is exactly what let the whole industry bet billions.

docs.title: What the scaling law is saying
docs.text: Plot both loss and compute on logarithmic axes and the measured points land almost on a straight line (Figure 1-24) — that is the scaling law. What it means in practice: to test whether a bigger model is better, you don't have to build it; read the line and you can quote a price.

docs.title: The 2022 correction: invest on both sides
docs.text: Compute gets spent in two places: parameters (brain capacity) and data (the textbooks). The 2022 Chinchilla work corrected the earlier imbalance — given a fixed compute budget, parameters and data should be scaled up in proportion, with roughly 20 words of text per parameter [25] (Figure 1-25). Earlier large models generally had "a huge brain and too little reading"; the same compute could have bought a lower loss.

docs.title: Built-in limitations: diminishing returns and the data wall
docs.text:
A power law is a curve that flattens (a straight line in log-log, increasingly flat in ordinary coordinates): the loss is still falling, but each equal drop in loss costs several times the input (Figure 1-26). A harder constraint is the data wall — high-quality public text is close to exhausted, so the "feed it more data" leg stops first [25].

Common misconceptions

Two of them. One: "the scaling law is a law" — it is an empirical regularity, not a law of physics; change the data quality or the architecture and the curve moves. Two: "falling loss = capability rising in proportion" — loss is only a proxy, and some capabilities (reasoning, multi-step calculation) appear more abruptly and are harder to predict. That is called emergence, and it is itself contested.

docs.title: Summary and self-check
docs.text:
Three sentences: loss against compute is close to a straight line on log-log axes, and that is what the industry dares to bet on; the budget has to be split in proportion between parameters and data; the flattening curve and the data wall show that "bigger" is no perpetual motion machine.

Two self-check questions:

  1. A company doubles its compute. Under Chinchilla, should it double parameters, double data, or double only one?
  2. Why does the data wall push the industry to research synthetic data and small models? (Hint: which of the two legs stops first?)

docs.title: Attention: letting every word look back for answers
The one-line intuition
docs.text: A word's meaning depends on the other words in the sentence. Attention lets every word question all the words and retrieve information by relevance — it turns "context" from a vague notion into a weighted average you can compute in parallel.

docs.title: An analogy: a meeting
docs.text: Reading "Xiaoming left his homework in the classroom", when you hear "it" you look back for what it refers to, and when you hear "left" you ask what was left — every word questions the other words and retrieves information by relevance. Attention turns this moment of mental activity into an arithmetic problem: query (what am I looking for), key (the label by which I can be found), value (the content I carry) [26].

docs.title: One attention step: take values by degree of match
docs.text: Figure 1-27 is one step end to end: the current word issues a query, each word shows its key, a dot product gives the degree of match, softmax normalises it into percentages, and the values of all words are summed with those weights. The output is "the new representation this word should have under these conditions". The idea was born for translation — letting each word of the translation look back at the relevant part of the source [27].

docs.title: Multi-head: several pairs of eyes, each looking at its own thing
docs.text: There are many kinds of relation between one word and another: grammatical collocation, reference, modification... Multi-head means running several independent attentions side by side, each watching its own relations, with outputs concatenated (Figure 1-28). The division of labour between heads is not assigned by hand; it grows by itself during training.

docs.title: Compared with recurrent networks: Chinese whispers vs a round table
docs.text: The champion before attention was the recurrent network (RNN): read word by word, each step getting only a summary compressed from the previous word, so distant information wears away along the way, and a hundred steps must be computed in order. Attention lets any two words connect directly (Figure 1-29): information doesn't wear away, and computation can be parallel — exactly the promise in the title of that 2017 paper, "Attention Is All You Need" [26].

docs.title: Built-in limitations: quadratic complexity
docs.text:
A hundred words connected pairwise is 100×100 relations; double the context and the computation quadruples. This is both why long contexts are expensive and the problem that Section 1.5.3 (compressing history into a fixed state) and Section 1.8 (the KV cache) set out to solve.

Common misconceptions

The belief that "attention = human attention". It is just the name of an arithmetic operation, "take a weighted sum of values by degree of match"; the seemingly "focused" patterns on a heatmap are a by-product of optimisation, unrelated to the physiology of human attention [26].

docs.title: Summary and self-check
docs.text:
Three sentences: attention = every word questions the other words and retrieves information weighted by match; multi-head lets different relations be watched separately; against recurrent networks it wins on both undamaged information and parallelism, at the price of quadratic complexity.

Two self-check questions:

  1. Context doubles from 4,000 tokens to 8,000 — how many times does the attention computation grow?
  2. Why does attention "solve the information wear of recurrent networks"? (Hint: the connections in Figure 1-29.)

Maths note. One attention step: \(\text{Attention}(Q,K,V)=\text{softmax}\!\left(\frac{QK^{\top}}{\sqrt{d}}\right)V\). \(Q\), \(K\) and \(V\) are the query, key and value matrices; \(\sqrt{d}\) is a scaling factor (it stops large dot products from pushing softmax into extreme distributions). Multi-head means doing this \(h\) times in parallel and concatenating.

docs.title: Linear attention and state space models: the RNN strikes back
The one-line intuition
docs.text: The quadratic complexity left by the previous section has a surprising solution: bring the old champion, the RNN, back. Take the softmax out of attention and the same network can be rewritten as an RNN that "carries a fixed state and recurs word by word" — constant cache, linear speed. This is the shared idea of linear attention and state space models (SSMs) [28][29].

docs.title: An analogy: meeting minutes
docs.text:
After a two-hour meeting you need to quote a sentence. You have two options: go through the whole recording (attention: exact, but you must play it all back); carry a single page of minutes (state: one page in your pocket, but details are compressed away).

Attention chooses to keep everything, with a cache that grows with the length of the meeting; RNNs/SSMs choose to keep only a summary, with a constant pocket. This section is about how to take the minutes so that less is lost.

docs.title: The problem it solves: one formula, two algorithms
docs.text:
Attention outputs a "weighted sum". Mathematically, once the softmax is removed, the expression "(QKᵀ)V" can be computed in a different order using associativity: first accumulate a state matrix from K and V, then query it with Q (Figure 1-31). The result is identical, but the second order can recur step by step — a word arrives, the state is updated once, no need to look back over all history.

The recurrent version is an RNN: fixed state size, constant memory, linear speed. It trains like attention (parallel) and infers like an RNN (thrifty with memory) — one network, two forms.

docs.title: State space models: making "what to remember" learnable
docs.text: SSMs write the recurrence in a more general form: new state = decay of the old state + injection of the new input, with how much to decay and how much to inject learned by the network itself. RWKV rewrites attention into a purely recurrent form [30]; Mamba adds "selectivity" to the state — the current input decides what gets written into the state and what is discarded [29], which is exactly how you learn "which line belongs in the minutes".

docs.title: Built-in limitations: exact recall is the weak spot
docs.text:
A fixed state is one sheet of paper: write a hundred thousand words of history into it and the sheet is still that size. Ask it to "find a particular sentence verbatim in a long document" and a pure SSM often fails — the detail has been compressed away. Attention, which looks back over the full history, is strong at finding details.

So the mainstream after 2025 is not replacement but hybrids: most layers use cheap linear/SSM layers for long-range continuity, a few layers use attention for exact recall (Figure 1-32).

Common misconceptions

The belief that "SSMs will replace attention". The popularity of hybrid architectures shows precisely that the two are complements: one handles cheap long-range memory, the other expensive exact recall. Replacement theories appear every few months, yet the hybrid share keeps growing.

docs.title: Summary and self-check
docs.text:
Three sentences: remove the softmax and attention can be rewritten as a recurrence with a fixed state; SSMs make "what to remember" learnable; pure SSMs lose on exact recall, and the mainstream answer is hybrid architecture.

Two self-check questions:

  1. At a context of 100k tokens, roughly how many times larger is the pure-attention cache than a fixed state? (An order-of-magnitude estimate is enough.)
  2. Why is a hybrid architecture more reliable than a pure SSM at tasks like "find a particular clause verbatim in a contract"?

Maths note. Recurrence: \(h_t = A\,h_{t-1} + B\,x_t\), output \(y_t = C\,h_t\); \(A\) is the decay (learnable), \(B\) the injection. Linear attention (no softmax) satisfies \(y_t = Q_t \sum_{i\le t} K_i^\top V_i = Q_t\, S_t\), where \(S_t = S_{t-1} + K_t^\top V_t\) — that is the "state accumulation" form.

docs.title: From images to language: diffusion models
The one-line intuition
docs.text: Autoregressive models write one word at a time going forward; diffusion models take another road: start with a blob of noise, then remove the noise step by step, and after a few dozen steps the content appears (Figure 1-33). They were originally the mainstay of image generation, and since 2025 they have broken into language generation too — because "parallel" is too tempting a word.

docs.title: An analogy: developing a photograph
docs.text: Diffusion works like developing film: the image is not drawn in one stroke but emerges gradually in the developer. Each step does one small thing — "take a little of this layer of fog away". During training every step of the reverse process has a known answer (because the model added the fog itself), so practice questions are endless and automatically generated [31].

docs.title: The problem it solves: breaking "get it right in one go" into "fix a little each time"
docs.text:
