Training takes the left path: add noise to a clear image step by step until it is pure noise — what was added at each step is fully known, and the network's job is to learn "subtract that bit". Generation takes the right path: start from pure noise, use the learned "denoising craft" in reverse, and after a few dozen steps the image appears.

Break one big task into hundreds of small ones, each easy to learn — that is the core reason diffusion can draw detail.

docs.title: Conditioning: glance at the prompt at every step
docs.text: "What to draw" is decided by the prompt: every step of the denoising network receives the prompt's vector [32]. During training the prompt is randomly blanked out, so the network learns both "draw unconditionally" and "draw under a condition", and the difference between the two is used to amplify the prompt's influence — one of the key tricks behind text-to-image quality.

docs.title: From images to language: parallel decoding
docs.text: Language diffusion (LLaDA [33], Mercury [34]) moves the same game to text: the whole sentence starts as placeholders, the model changes several positions at once each step, and after a few steps it converges on the complete text (Figure 1-34). Autoregressive generation of n characters needs at least n steps; diffusion can produce a whole passage in a few dozen — which is why the selling point of diffusion language models is "twice the tokens per second".

docs.title: Built-in limitations: coherence and step count
docs.text:
Parallel rewriting saves steps but also loses one natural advantage of autoregression: writing left to right, earlier text naturally constrains later text. Diffusion needs more steps and better training to match the coherence of long passages; cut the steps too far and quality drops at once — the trade-off between steps and latency is its own "scaling law".

Common misconceptions

The belief that "diffusion models can only draw pictures". It is a generative paradigm, and images, audio, video, protein structures and text all have diffusion implementations. Paradigm and modality are two different things.

docs.title: Summary and self-check
docs.text:
Three sentences: diffusion splits generation into a few hundred steps of "remove a bit of noise", with training examples generated automatically; conditional generation looks at the prompt at every step; moved to language, parallel decoding buys speed at the cost of harder long-text coherence.

Two self-check questions:

  1. Why can diffusion's training data be "generated automatically without limit", while labels for supervised learning cannot?
  2. For an application that must "quote a contract clause exactly, word for word", what risk does autoregression carry, and what risk does diffusion?

Maths note. Forward noising: \(q(x_t \mid x_{t-1}) = \mathcal{N}\!\left(\sqrt{1-\beta_t}\,x_{t-1},\ \beta_t I\right)\), where \(\beta_t\) is the noise strength at step \(t\). The reverse process \(p_\theta(x_{t-1}\mid x_t)\) that the network learns uses the same \(\beta_t\), so the training objective (predict the noise added at each step) has an analytic answer.

docs.title: Making it behave: alignment, hallucination and safety
The one-line intuition
docs.text:
The model that left the factory in Section 1.5 only knows how to "continue web pages" — ask it a question and it may well invent ten similar questions. Between "can talk" and "actually useful" lies a stretch of factory education: first demonstration, then fine-tuning. And the two problems this education cannot fix — hallucination and jailbreaks — each have their own mechanistic roots.

This section answers the three most common questions: why can it "answer questions"? Why does it say things that are confidently wrong? What do the safety guardrails actually block, and what do they cost?

docs.title: An analogy: onboarding a new employee
docs.text:
Pretraining is like reading every document the company has amassed over ten years — astonishing breadth, but a feral way of working: ask it to "write an apology letter to a customer" and it may hand you an "analysis of apology-letter writing techniques". Supervised fine-tuning is like learning the job from a mentor: studying dozens of demonstrations of "here is how you handle this situation", until it looks like an assistant. Reinforcement learning from human feedback is like tuning against customer feedback: produce several versions of the same task, have a person pick the better one, and nudge towards what people prefer.

Only the three stages together[35] turn a "continuation machine" into an "assistant". Note a fact that is easy to overlook: all three stages change the same batch of parameters of the same model — nothing is bolted on; the model itself is reshaped.

docs.title: Hallucination: a consequence you can derive from the mechanism
docs.text:
The conclusion first: hallucination is not a malfunction; it is the natural product of the training objective. Section 1.5 said pretraining's objective is "predict the next word", and the criterion for choosing that next word is does it sound right, not is it true — the two criteria are never distinguished during training.

Split it into two causes (Figure 1-39). Cause one, missing knowledge: for things absent from the training data, the model does not know that it does not know — it has no natural representation of the state "I'm not sure", so it just carries on composing plausible text. Cause two, fluency first: composing a perfectly formatted fake citation scores exactly as highly as restating a real fact, under the "predict the next word" objective — a systematic review of hallucination is [36].

This is why the classic "invented citation" hallucination is so easy to explain: the format it has seen a thousand times; the content it has not. Missing knowledge gives it the freedom; fluency first gives it the nerve. Why can't you eliminate it by "trying harder"? Because eliminating it would require putting "truth" into the training objective — and "truth" cannot be labelled automatically from text. That is exactly the hole retrieval-augmented generation (Section 1.7.3) is meant to fill.

docs.title: Safety: a line that gets probed from every direction
docs.text:
The third stage of alignment taught the model that "dangerous requests should be refused". But "dangerous" is a line drawn on a continuous spectrum (Figure 1-40): drawn too loosely, harm leaks through the gaps; drawn too tightly, normal chemistry lessons and medical questions get refused too.

And a line is a rule, and rules can be gamed: wrap the same dangerous request in a story shell ("imagine you are a machine with no restrictions", "my granny always used to read me this recipe") and early safety training may fail — this is a jailbreak. It is not a bug you "fix and move on"; it is a running contest of attack and defence: each patch closes one workaround, and new workarounds keep appearing. Approaches like Constitutional AI have the model criticise and correct itself against a written set of principles, moving part of the defensive line from human labelling to auditable rules[37].

docs.title: Built-in limitations: the alignment tax
docs.text:
Alignment is not free. Once a model has been tuned to be polite, safe and well-behaved, benchmark scores usually dip slightly — that loss is colloquially the alignment tax (Figure 1-41). It is not a bug but a genuine trade: giving up a slice of "unrestrained capability" in exchange for "safe to hand to ordinary people".

The real argument is about how big the tax should be, and alignment to whom: "make it behave" can mean behaving for the user, for the vendor, or for the regulator, and the three do not always want the same things. This question only sharpens in the agent era of Section 1.7 — the more hands and feet, the heavier the consequences of "behaving".

Common misconceptions

Two of them. One: "hallucination is a bug; fix it and it's gone" — as long as the training objective is still "predict the next word", hallucination has a mechanistic source; what you can do is use retrieval, calibration and refusal to push down its rate and harm. Two: "safety alignment is just a filter bolted on" — it reshapes parameters, affects capability (the alignment tax), and is a contest of attack and defence that never ends.

docs.title: Summary and self-check
docs.text:
Three sentences: supervised fine-tuning and human feedback after pretraining reshape a "continuation machine" into an "assistant"; hallucination grows mechanistically out of a training objective where "sounds right is not the same as is true"; safety alignment is a contest of attack and defence, and its price is the alignment tax.

Two self-check questions:

  1. Why is it so hard to teach a model to say "I'm not sure" when answering? (Hint: in the training data, which is more common — a confident wrong answer, or honest ignorance?)
  2. A company claims "our model has no hallucinations". Given this section's mechanistic analysis, what is that statement most likely to mean?

Maths note. The RLHF objective is usually written as: \(\max_\pi\ \mathbb{E}_{x\sim\pi}\,[r(x)] - \beta\,\mathrm{KL}(\pi \,\|\, \pi_{\text{ref}})\) — maximise the human-preference reward \(r\) while the KL term tethers the model to the reference model \(\pi_{\text{ref}}\), stopping it from drifting away to please the rater. The larger \(\beta\), the heavier the alignment tax.

docs.title: Agents
docs.text: What separates a model that can only answer questions from an assistant that can finish the job for you? Not, mostly, being "smarter" — mostly hands and feet: it can call tools, remember context, and break one job into several steps and carry them out. This chapter is about the engineering that turns a "model" into an "agent" — fitting the hands and feet first (the harness), then how to make it better and better at the work (RSI and multi-agent), and finally how it borrows tools and knowledge from outside (MCP, skills, retrieval).

docs.title: The model's hands and feet: the harness
The one-line intuition
docs.text:
Between the assistant you use in a product and the bare "predict the next word" model of Section 1.5 sits a layer of engineering called the harness. What it adds is not intelligence but hands, eyes and memory: it can call tools, see the results, and remember last time's decision.

"Model + harness = agent" — the other two sections of this chapter are all about the advanced moves of that harness layer.

docs.title: What the bare model lacks
docs.text: A bare model has only one channel: text in, text out. It says "I've deleted that file", but it has no hands — saying it's done and it being done are the same act to it. Nor has it any memory: anything outside this conversation does not exist. The harness supplies exactly these things.

docs.title: The agent loop: observe → decide → call → feed back
docs.text:
At the heart of the harness is a loop (Figure 1-45): the model reads the context once (observe) and decides what to do next (decide) — which may be to answer, or to call a tool; the harness runs the tool and feeds the result back into the context; then round again.

The loop produces a change of kind, not an addition: a model on its own cannot "read a file", and the loop plus tools lets it — the capability comes from the combination of "model + tools + loop", not from more model parameters. Early work like ReAct showed exactly this: let the model "think while doing, look at the result and think again", and the same parameters become dramatically more usable[38]; SWE-agent later wrapped that loop around software-engineering tools and could fix real GitHub issues on its own[39].

docs.title: Built-in limitations: the context budget
docs.text:
Every "observe" in the loop re-reads the whole context (Figure 1-46): the system prompt is fixed rent, the history grows with every exchange, a single page of tool output can be thousands of tokens, and blank space must be kept for the answer. The daily engineering of a harness is managing this memory: what comes in, what gets compressed, what gets dropped.

Common misconceptions

That the harness "bolts intelligence onto the model". Quite the opposite: everything inside a harness is deterministic engineering — file reads and writes, command execution, string concatenation. All the intelligence comes from the model; all the reliability comes from the engineering, and the cleaner that boundary, the easier the system is to maintain.

docs.title: Summary and self-check
docs.text:
Three sentences: the harness fits the model with hands, eyes and memory; the agent loop (observe-decide-call-feed back) changes capability in kind; the context window is the loop's hard constraint, and managing it is the harness's main engineering job.

Two self-check questions:

  1. Why is "I've fixed the code" from a model completely different in credibility from "the file really was changed" in the harness?
  2. A task has gone round 40 times without finishing. What constraint is it most likely to hit first?

Maths note. No formulas in this section. One engineering fact: the attention cost for a context window of n is O(n²) (Section 1.5.2), so "40 turns, re-reading the whole history each time" accumulates cost quadratically.

docs.title: Improving the agent: RSI and multi-agent
The one-line intuition
docs.text: There are two ways to make an agent stronger, and neither needs you to write more code: self-improvement (RSI) — use the current model to produce data, and train a better model from it; and multi-agent — several models dividing the work. Both are genuinely effective and both have clear failure points; the discipline of this section is: for every advantage, name when it stops holding.

docs.title: Self-improvement: how the flywheel turns, and where it stops
docs.text:
The bootstrap flywheel (Figure 1-47): the current model generates solutions → keep only those that pass verification → train on them → the stronger model generates harder problems[40]. It really does turn in maths and code — because right and wrong can be checked automatically.

And "self-improvement" does not only happen at the model layer (retraining weights): the prompt and policy layer (writing lessons learned back into the system prompt), the tool and harness layer (giving the agent the one tool it most lacks) and the curriculum layer (making the next round of tasks harder automatically) are all RSI. Same mechanism — produce, verify, feed back — only the place it feeds back to differs.

That is also where it fails: in domains with no verifier, the flywheel will not turn. Quality of prose, taste in a design, have no automatic scorer; when a model "grades itself", the data it produces trains a more confident model, not a more correct one — self-infatuation, the degradation most worth guarding against in any discussion of RSI.

docs.title: Multi-agent: division of labour, debate, market
docs.text:
Multi-agent splits a task across several models: pipeline (write, review and revise each own a stage), debate (proposer and critic pick holes in each other, a judge sums up), market (agents with different specialisms claim tasks). The value of debate is fewer blind spots; the value of a market is specialisation[41].

But collaboration has its own cost: one more agent means one more context to keep in sync, and one more chance to garble the message. Under what conditions is multi-agent actually stronger? The task splits cleanly, intermediate results can be verified, and coordination costs less than the division of labour gains — miss any one and it merely amplifies cost and confusion (Figure 1-48).

docs.title: Built-in limitations: past the complexity line
docs.text:
The benefit curve is not monotonic: for simple tasks multi-agent is a pure loss (coordination overhead), at medium complexity it pulls ahead, and past the complexity line it is dragged down by its own confusion — a message passed between agents distorts with every hop, structurally the same as the Chinese-whispers game from Section 1.5.2. The practical discipline: push a single agent to its limit first, then split; do not start with multi-agent.

Common misconceptions

That "multi-agent = a smarter team". Agents do not truly "understand each other"; they exchange text, and text passed through N hands picks up N layers of distortion. Multi-agent is essentially task decomposition in engineering, not an anthropomorphic team.

docs.title: Summary and self-check
docs.text:
Three sentences: RSI turns the flywheel with an automatic verifier, and domains without one drift into self-infatuation; the three multi-agent topologies each have their fit, given a task that splits, results that can be verified, and low coordination cost; either way, push a single agent to its limit first.

Two self-check questions:

  1. "Have the model score its own essay, then train on the scores" — what is this flywheel missing?
  2. A five-agent system completes a task a single agent could not, at six times the cost. What signal tells you it's time to go back and retry with a single agent?

Maths note. No formulas in this section. One useful quantity: if each agent's reliability is p, then in a pipeline topology the reliability of the whole chain is p to the power k (k being the number of stages) — the more you divide the work, the more reliable each stage must be. That is the hidden tax of multi-agent design.

docs.title: 1.7.3 MCP, skills, embeddings and knowledge bases
Extending the agent: MCP, skills, embeddings and knowledge bases
The one-line intuition
docs.text: The harness fitted the model with hands; this section is about how far those hands can reach: connecting to tools (MCP, a common protocol), to methods (skills, instruction sheets loaded on demand), and to knowledge (embeddings and retrieval). All three answer one question: how does the world outside the model get plugged in cheaply.

docs.title: MCP: turning M×N wiring into M+N
docs.text:
Without a common protocol, connecting M assistants to N tools means writing M×N pieces of bespoke glue — every vendor inventing its own interface. MCP (Model Context Protocol) standardises the interface: the assistant implements a client once, the tool implements a server once, and in between they speak the same protocol[42].

M+N replaces M×N — and the value of a standard interface is far greater than the interface itself: adding a new tool goes from "start a development project" to "change one line of config". Structurally the same as the history of USB: before the standard, every peripheral had its own port.

docs.title: Skills: instruction sheets borrowed on demand
docs.text:
Cram every operating instruction into the context and you soon burn through the budget of Section 1.7.1, and most of it has nothing to do with the current task. The skills answer: keep only a one-line catalogue resident in the context ("skills A/B/C exist, here's what each covers"), fetch the full text only when the matching job comes up, and drop it again afterwards.

Which makes the difference from a prompt clear: a prompt is the speech you carry every time; a skill is a book borrowed from the library when needed. "Load on demand" is the crux — it lets an agent command a hundred methods without having to carry a hundred methods at once.

docs.title: Retrieval augmentation: look it up first, then answer
docs.text:
The mechanistic root of hallucination (Section 1.6) is "making it up from parameter memory". Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) takes another route: encode the question as a vector, fetch the few passages in the knowledge base that are closest in meaning, and hand both the material and the question to the model — so it speaks from the material rather than from memory[43].

"Closest in meaning" works thanks to embeddings: the "everything is a list of numbers" planted in Section 1.3.2 unfolds here — training brings texts with similar meaning close together in vector space (Figure 1-52), so retrieval collapses into the simple geometry of "find the nearest neighbours".

docs.title: Built-in limitations: retrieval eases hallucination, it does not cure it
docs.text:
Three residual risks: if the material isn't there, it still makes things up (when retrieval comes back empty, the model falls back to memory mode); if retrieval is wrong, the answer is wrong ("similar meaning" can fetch an irrelevant passage); the material itself can be wrong (RAG is faithful to its sources, not a guarantee that they are true). RAG pushes hallucination from "uncontrollable" to "auditable" — a change of kind, but not down to zero.

Common misconceptions

That "once you add RAG, the model learns from the live internet". The knowledge base is a static snapshot; it does not update with model training. RAG changes "what it looks at when answering", not "what the model knows". The distinction was settled long ago in the training/inference framing of Section 1.3.4.

docs.title: Summary and self-check
docs.text:
Three sentences: MCP turns M×N wiring into M+N with a common protocol; skills solve the context budget with "catalogue resident, body on demand"; RAG eases hallucination with "look it up first, then speak" but does not cure it.

Two self-check questions:

  1. Why is "the value of a standard interface far greater than the interface itself"? Give a structurally similar example from outside this book.
  2. An enterprise knowledge base updates every three days. What happens when the RAG system is asked "what was concluded in today's meeting"?

Maths note. Embedding retrieval: the document and the question are each encoded as vectors \(\mathbf{d}_i, \mathbf{q}\), and you take the k with the largest cosine similarity \(\cos(\mathbf{q},\mathbf{d}_i)=\frac{\mathbf{q}\cdot\mathbf{d}_i}{\|\mathbf{q}\|\|\mathbf{d}_i\|}\). An approximate nearest-neighbour index (such as HNSW) brings a query down from "compare against every document" to "compare against a small subset".

docs.title: Deploying a model: homogeneous, heterogeneous, precision and the KV cache
The one-line intuition
docs.text: All the "training" and "inference" of previous chapters has to land on a real chip in the end. This section answers the last common question: why is it so expensive and so slow — and which levers engineers use to make it cheaper and faster.

docs.title: Homogeneous and heterogeneous: the all-rounder versus the specialist team
docs.text:
A CPU is homogeneous computing: a few dozen identical all-rounder cores that can do anything — logic, branches, serial work. A GPU is the heterogeneous idea: thousands of tiny cores, each only able to do one simple thing (multiply and add), but all at once.

The bulk of a neural network's work is massively independent multiply-adds — matrix multiplication. That "dumb labour" happens to be the GPU's natural gift. Which is why graphics cards became a strategic material in the AI era: not because the card is magic, but because the task and the tool happen to fit.

docs.title: Precision: how many bits each number gets
docs.text:
Every parameter in the model is a number, stored by default as 32-bit floating point (fp32). But inference does not actually need that resolution: 16 bits (fp16/bf16) is nearly lossless, 8 bits (fp8) is common, and 4-bit integers (int4) is the key rung where "will it fit at all" is traded against "quality drops a little"[44][45].

Quantization (squeezing high-precision numbers into low precision) pays off directly: VRAM goes from 4 units down to 0.5. The price is coarser numbers — in the extreme, the rarest knowledge is the first to be erased.

docs.title: The KV cache: the physical bottleneck of long conversations
docs.text: Section 1.5.2 said attention pairs everything with everything; at inference time, to avoid recomputation, the keys and values of every past turn have to stay in VRAM — that is the KV cache, and it grows linearly with context length. A long conversation can eat your VRAM before it gets to the point.

docs.title: The memory wall: three bills added together
docs.text: At inference, three things live in VRAM: weights (the resident bulk), activations (intermediate computation), and the KV cache (growing with the conversation) — the foreshadowing planted in Section 1.3.4 merges here into the full ledger of "the memory wall". Each of the three levers answers one bill: quantization squeezes the weights, batching spreads the activations, window and cache management squeeze the KV; the fixed state of Section 1.5.3 is a more aggressive move.

docs.title: Built-in limitations: every optimisation is a trade
docs.text:
Quantization costs precision, batching costs latency variance, compressing the context costs detail. There are no free levers, only explicitly accepted costs — the whole of deployment engineering is choosing the right costs for the business.

Common misconceptions

That "a big model is necessarily slow". Inference speed depends at once on parameter count, precision, batch size, context length and architecture (the parallel decoding of Section 1.5.4) — "big and fast" and "small and slow" both exist; what matters is the whole engineering chain.

docs.title: Summary and self-check
docs.text:
Three sentences: the main work of a neural network is matrix multiplication, which happens to fit the GPU's heterogeneous architecture; quantization trades precision for VRAM and is the key deployment lever; the KV cache grows linearly with context and is the physical bottleneck of long conversations.

Two self-check questions:

  1. When the context doubles, which bill in VRAM grows? Which stays the same?
  2. Why does "the rarest knowledge disappear first" after int4 quantization? (Hint: recall the manifold of Section 1.3.3 — rare points live where it is thinnest.)

Maths note. fp32 is 32 bits per number; int4 is 4 bits per number, an 8× compression of VRAM. Quantization is essentially mapping continuous values onto the \(2^4=16\) levels that 4 bits can represent, and the mapping rules (symmetric/asymmetric, per-layer/per-group scaling) are where the various methods differ[44].

docs.title: Computing and development basics
docs.text: This part does not teach you to write code. It explains why the tools you use every day exist, and what problem each of them is solving.

docs.title: What a program is: from source code to running
The one-line intuition
docs.text: A program is a piece of text written for a machine, plus a conveyor belt that turns it into machine actions. Every tool in this chapter exists to serve one station on that belt.

docs.title: The whole chain: from text to process
docs.text:
What you write is called source code — text a human can read. A compiler translates it into machine instructions and runs a large batch of checks along the way; the result is an executable file you can run directly; once launched — by double-clicking or from the command line — it becomes something active in memory: a process.

Each of the three abstractions maps to one thing inside the machine. Memorise this table and every tool that follows becomes easy to understand:

A variable is a slot in memory — it has a name, a type and an address. A function is a stretch of instructions you can jump to again and again — give it input, it gives you output. A file is a named run of bytes on disk — it survives a shutdown.

docs.title: Compiled versus interpreted: translate the whole book first, or interpret sentence by sentence
docs.text: Some languages translate the whole book first, then run it (C, Rust): fast to run, and errors surface early. Others read and execute as they go (Python, JS): edit and run immediately, but an error only blows up when execution reaches that line. Most modern languages are hybrids: Python compiles to bytecode before executing, and Java still compiles just-in-time at runtime. The boundary is a spectrum, not a binary; what really decides the choice is how often you need to change the code and how fast you need it to run.

docs.title: What happens in the stack when a function is called
docs.text: Every call to a function stacks another "frame" in memory: it holds the function's arguments, its local variables, and where to go back to when it is done. When the function returns, the frame is removed. Nested calls are stacked frames; a "stack overflow" means the frames piled past the ceiling — usually meaning some function has been calling itself without end.

docs.title: Built-in limitations: every station on the chain can fail
docs.text:
Source code can have syntax errors; a compiler cannot spot logic errors while translating; and at runtime there are errors that only blow up on particular data. Each kind of error belongs to one station — which is why a toolchain needs a compiler (to catch compile errors), tests (to catch logic errors) and a debugger (to catch runtime errors): one net per station.

Common misconceptions

Thinking "a program = a source code file". Source code is only the text at the starting point; what actually runs is a process — it has memory, has state, and dies. Understanding that "the code in the file" and "the process in memory" are two different worlds is the precondition for understanding every development tool.

docs.title: Summary and self-check
docs.text:
Three sentences: a program is source code turned into an executable by a compiler, which becomes a process when run; variables, functions and files map to memory slots, jumpable instructions and named bytes; compiled versus interpreted is a trade-off about when to translate.

Two questions to check yourself:

  1. "The program crashed" and "the program won't compile" — at which station of the chain does each error occur?
  2. Why are interpreted languages naturally suited to fast trial and error?

Maths note. No formulas in this section. One fact about orders of magnitude: a modern CPU executes billions of instructions per second, while a person reads code at a few dozen lines per second — a machine's "step" is eight orders of magnitude faster than a person's. That is why performance problems are almost always "the wrong order of magnitude", never "just a little short".

docs.title: Tracking changes like snapshots: Git and Git clients
The one-line intuition
docs.text: Git takes snapshots of a project: each commit records "what every file looks like right now" and remembers which snapshot came before it. The whole history is an append-only graph — that is the entire basis for "you can change things boldly".

docs.title: The commit chain: an append-only graph
docs.text: Each commit is a snapshot plus a pointer to the previous commit. From any commit you can follow the pointers back through the entire history — nothing can be deleted or overwritten. Two parallel attempts (branches) can be merged at their tips: a merge commit has two "parents" and remembers both sides at once[46].

docs.title: Three areas: change → pick → save
docs.text: The daily flow has three steps: make a mess in the working tree (that is fine) → use git add to pick changes into the staging area → use git commit to save them. The staging area's value is often underestimated: it lets commits be grouped by logic rather than by time — one commit telling one story is the baseline for readable history.

docs.title: The two shapes of merging
docs.text: If the main line never moved, the pointer simply slides to the new tip (fast-forward). If both sides moved, Git creates a new commit with two parents (three-way merge). If both sides changed the same line, Git does not guess — it marks the conflict and leaves the ruling to a human. A conflict is not a malfunction; it is the system saying "this step needs human judgement".

docs.title: Git clients: no need to memorise commands
docs.text: The command line is the underlying truth, but you need not live in it. Graphical clients turn add/commit/merge into visible operations, and an IDE's built-in Git panel joins "edit — view the diff — commit" into one continuous flow. Build your intuition with a client first; the command line can fill in any time — both operate on the same repository, so mixing them is harmless.

docs.title: Auditable: who, when, and what changed
docs.text: Every commit carries its author and timestamp — when something goes wrong you can answer precisely who changed that line, and when. Turn on signed commits and each commit also carries a private-key signature, so whoever receives the source can verify that the code has not been tampered with since the committer signed it. Snapshot + signature + timeline make up the audit chain of the source — that is exactly how this book's sample chapter is kept.

docs.title: Built-in limitations: snapshots record content, not intent
docs.text:
Git remembers what every version looked like, but not why — "why it was changed this way" lives only in the commit message, and the commit message is hand-written. The ceiling on readable history is set by commit discipline (one thing per commit, and say clearly why). The other boundary is file type. Git's diff and merge are designed around lines and work best on plain text: code, configuration, Markdown, LaTeX and CSV can all be tracked line by line; complex packaged formats such as MS Office are mostly beyond it; a non-scanned PDF with a text layer can just about be tracked, while a scan is no different from an image. Binary files can be snapshotted but not diffed line by line, and the repository balloons quickly — that kind of content needs a dedicated storage scheme.

Common misconceptions

Thinking "Git is for programmers only". The snapshot + pointer model holds for any text that changes: papers, contracts, configuration, ledgers. This book's sample chapters live in Git too — every page you are reading has a complete change history you can consult.

docs.title: Summary and self-check
docs.text:
Three sentences: Git's history is an append-only graph of snapshots; the three-area flow lets commits be grouped by logic; in the two shapes of merging, a conflict is a question left for a human.

Two questions to check yourself:

  1. Why does the staging area improve the quality of the commit history?
  2. Two branches changed different parts of the same function — will merging conflict? What if they changed the same line?

Maths note. No formulas in this section. One structural fact: commit history is a directed acyclic graph (DAG) — "acyclic" guarantees that following pointers never loops back to where you started, which is the structural guarantee that "history cannot be scrambled".

docs.title: Programming tools: the IDE and the toolchain
The one-line intuition
docs.text: The four core tools of writing programs — editor, compiler, debugger, version control — are each independent; an IDE merely puts them into one window and makes them aware of each other. Once you understand how the four work together, no button in an IDE is a mystery.

docs.title: How the four tools work together
docs.text: The editor handles writing and changing; the compiler handles translating and checking; the debugger lets the program stop halfway so you can see the real state in memory; version control remembers every step and lets you roll back when something breaks. The four loop together: change code → the compiler reports an error → read the error → locate it → it passes → commit.

docs.title: The command-line combination and the IDE are equivalent
docs.text: A command-line veteran does the same job with separate tools: an editor (Vim/Emacs) + a compiler driven from the prompt + a debugger (GDB) + Git. Both ways drive the same underlying tools; the difference is only interface and degree of automation. An IDE's real advantage is not "more features" but eliminating copy-and-paste: an error jumps straight to the line of code, a breakpoint hangs directly in the editor.

docs.title: One edit-compile-debug cycle
docs.text: The habit a beginner most needs to practise hides inside this loop: the compiler's error message is not an accusation, it is a clue. After step ② reports an error, step ③ is not "recompile and hope", but read the message, locate the cause, understand it — once that step is mastered, the toolchain truly works for you.

docs.title: Built-in limitations: tools hide details on your behalf
docs.text:
Autocomplete and one-click run let a beginner go a long time without knowing "what happens underneath". That is fine day to day, and then you are caught out the moment something breaks — because you are not facing code, you are facing a black box. This book's advice: use an IDE, but know which of the four tools stands behind each button.

Common misconceptions

Thinking "the tool decides your level". Tools decide the floor and the comfort; the ceiling is decided by your understanding of the chain in Section 2.1 — someone for whom the chain is clear can pick up any toolchain within a day.

docs.title: Summary and self-check
docs.text:
Three sentences: the four tools each cover one stage, and the IDE is their integrator; the edit-compile-debug loop is the daily rhythm, and error messages are clues, not accusations; tools hide details, but someone who understands the chain is not afraid to switch tools.

Two questions to check yourself:

  1. Behind "go to definition" in an IDE, what does the toolchain actually do?
  2. Why is "reading compiler errors" the highest-return habit for a beginner?

Maths note. No formulas in this section. One engineering fact: "jump to definition" and autocomplete in a modern IDE depend on a language server — a service that parses source code into an index and sits resident in the background. That design (decoupling the language from the editor) is the precedent, in developer tools, for the "unified interface" idea discussed in Section 1.7.3.

docs.title: The one-line intuition
docs.text: Modern programs are almost all assembled: your code plus dozens of libraries other people wrote. A package manager is the automated assembler — declare whom you depend on, and it downloads, installs and picks the right versions. Its entire reason for existing: manual assembly inevitably spins out of control once you pass three dependencies.

docs.title: The dependency tree and diamond dependencies
docs.text: Dependencies form a tree: your program depends on libraries A and B, and A and B each depend on others. The classic awkward shape is the diamond dependency — A and B depend on different versions of the same library. Which do you install? Two strategies: upgrade to a new version both sides accept, or unify the whole tree on one version and pray. The deeper the tree, the likelier a diamond appears — which is why "few dependencies" became a virtue.

docs.title: Semantic versioning: declaring breakage with numbers
docs.text: What makes a diamond negotiable is semantic versioning (semver), a convention: the version number has three parts — major.minor.patch. Major +1 means the interface changed (you must change code); minor +1 means a feature was added; patch +1 means a bug was fixed. So "depends on ≥2.3, <3.0" is an executable promise. The convention is worth only what everyone's adherence to it is worth — automatic upgrades are safe only in an ecosystem that keeps the promise.

docs.title: Package managers are a family
docs.text: "Package manager" does not name one piece of software but a layered family. The language and runtime layer manages each ecosystem's libraries — uv/pip for Python, cargo for Rust, pnpm/npm for JavaScript, NuGet/dotnet for .NET. The system layer manages the whole machine's software — zypper on openSUSE, apt on Debian-family systems, dnf on Fedora-family ones, pacman on Arch, winget/scoop on Windows, brew on macOS. And there is the more thorough declarative global layer — Nix and Guix (Section 2.6). Several layers often coexist on one machine: system packages via zypper, project dependencies via uv — clear layering with no crossing of boundaries is the first rule of a clean environment.

docs.title: Conflict resolution and lock files
docs.text: Beyond the two strategies for resolving conflicts, the lock file of Section 2.5 is a third: pin the resolution result (exact versions for the whole tree) so that "install once" and "install ten thousand times" give the same answer. Declaring dependencies is "what I want"; the lock file is "what was actually obtained" — keeping the two apart is what makes reproducibility possible.

docs.title: Built-in limitations: dependencies are borrowed trust
docs.text:
Every package you pull in brings its transitive dependencies — a ten-line utility library can drag in hundreds of indirect ones. Supply-chain attacks (a stolen author account, a malicious release) get in through exactly this chain of trust. So the engineering discipline is: a dependency is a liability, not an asset — with each one you add, ask "is this feature really worth another chain of trust?"

Common misconceptions

Thinking "package managers solved dependencies". They solved the automation of downloading and installing; version conflicts, breaking upgrades and supply-chain security still need conventions (semver), tools (lock files) and discipline (few dependencies) together. Tools turn chaos into something controllable; controllable is not the same as risk-free.

docs.title: Summary and self-check
docs.text:
Three sentences: package managers assemble dependencies automatically, and the deeper the tree the more diamonds; semver declares the degree of breakage in three numbers and is the precondition for automatic upgrades; the lock file pins the dependency tree, and is the foundation of reproducibility.

Two questions to check yourself:

  1. What does each of the two strategies for resolving a diamond dependency cost?
  2. Why is "few dependencies" still a virtue in the AI era? (Hint: think of the chain of trust in Section 1.7.3.)

Maths note. No formulas in this section. One combinatorial fact: if each package depends on three others on average and the tree is five levels deep, transitive dependencies can reach \(3^5 = 243\) in theory — the dependency tree grows exponentially, which explains why "one small project dragging in hundreds of packages" is normal.

docs.title: Keeping behaviour consistent: reproducibility and declarative tools
The one-line intuition
docs.text: "It runs on my machine" is the most famous sentence in engineering, and the weakest defence. Reproducibility has exactly one goal: the same inputs (code + dependencies + environment) produce exactly the same result, on any machine, at any time. It stands on two pillars: the lock file (Section 2.4) and declarative tools.

docs.title: First, meet the hash: a fingerprint for content
docs.text: The skeleton of a lock file is the hash. A hash function is like a juicer: it presses an input of any size (a file, a whole directory tree) into a short fingerprint of fixed length — with one decisive property: change one byte of the content and the fingerprint becomes unrecognisable, and there is currently no way to deliberately construct two inputs with the same fingerprint. So "same fingerprint" becomes a machine-checkable proof of "same content" — the lock files below, and the build outputs of Section 2.6, all stake everything on that property.

docs.title: The lock file: fingerprinting the whole tree
docs.text: As Section 2.4 said, the lock file pins every leaf of the dependency tree: an exact version plus a content hash. The hash is the content's fingerprint — if upstream quietly changes one byte, the fingerprint will not match and the install is refused outright. Reproducibility is therefore not "happens to be the same" but "forced to be the same".

docs.title: Declarative versus imperative: record the destination, not the steps
docs.text: Two philosophies of configuration. Imperative (traditional operations): record the steps — install this first, then edit that file; the steps live in someone's head, and drift between machines happens quietly. Declarative: record the destination — "this is the state I want", and the tool works out the path from the current state to it; the same declaration converges to the same result on any machine. Declarative knowledge lives in the repository: it can go into version control, be reviewed, be rolled back.

docs.title: Containers: package the environment and carry it with you
docs.text: Declarative configuration solves "what to install"; containers solve "how to carry it": pack the program together with all its dependencies into an image, and it behaves the same wherever it goes. Images also have a layered design — common base layers are shared by all images, and only the layers that changed need downloading again, which makes distribution cheap.

docs.title: Levels: reproducibility is stacked up layer by layer
docs.text: "Reproducible" is not a single switch but a set of layers, from the inside out: innermost is the language-level lock file (Section 2.4, pinning project dependencies); outside that, system package management (pinning the software list of the whole machine); outside that, container images (packaging the application with its environment as an immutable distribution unit — the industry standard is called OCI, and tools such as Docker follow it); outermost, a declarative operating system (Section 2.6), pinning the kernel and services along with everything else. The higher the level, the wider the scope of reproduction and the greater the investment — choose the level your needs require instead of always maxing out.

docs.title: Built-in limitations: reproducibility has a cost
docs.text:
Lock files need maintenance (dependency upgrades must be done deliberately rather than happening to you); declarative systems have a learning curve; container images expire (the dependencies inside them age too). Reproducibility is an ongoing investment, and what it buys is: a new machine usable within the hour, incidents that can be replayed exactly, and "it runs on my machine" becoming a valid defence from now on.

Common misconceptions

Thinking "reproducible = write the commands down". The commands you wrote down are an imperative recipe, and the machine's history will still make it drift. The test for reproducibility is hard: a different time, a different machine, byte-for-byte identical results — fall short of that and you still only have "happens to be the same".

docs.title: Summary and self-check
docs.text:
Three sentences: the lock file pins the dependency tree with hashes; declarative configuration records the destination rather than the steps, and the knowledge lives in the repository; containers package the environment to carry with you. Together the three turn "it runs on my machine" into "it runs anywhere".

Two questions to check yourself:

  1. Why can a content hash solve both "version drift" and "supply-chain poisoning" at once?
  2. A team of three, each with a different development machine. What does declarative configuration give the team in return?

Maths note. A content hash (such as SHA-256) maps any input to a fingerprint of fixed length: change one byte of input and the fingerprint becomes unrecognisable, and it is currently impossible to deliberately find two inputs with the same fingerprint. Equal hash ≈ equal content — that approximation is the trust foundation of modern software distribution.

docs.title: The operating system, reproducible like code: declarative operating systems
The one-line intuition
docs.text: The previous section made the application layer reproducible; this section pushes one level up to the top: the operating system itself can be managed declaratively. Systems such as NixOS and GNU Guix write "which packages to install, which services to run, who the users are" into a configuration file, and the whole system is built from that one declaration.

docs.title: Generations and atomic rollback
docs.text: Every change produces a new generation, and the old one is kept exactly as it was; "current" is just a pointer. Did the upgrade go wrong? Point the pointer back at the previous generation — a few seconds, an atomic operation, no need to "take it apart again". The confidence to upgrade boldly comes from rollback being cheap and complete — strikingly consistent with Git's commit philosophy (Section 2.2): immutable history + a movable pointer.

docs.title: Configuration and packages from the same source
docs.text: A deeper unification: package definitions, system configuration and build scripts are written in the same language. Change one parameter of a package and everything that depends on it gets rebuilt along with it — the system and its packages cannot quietly drift apart. Push the same configuration declaration to a laptop, a server and an old machine kept for rescue work, and all three converge on the same state (Figure 1-58).

docs.title: Operations compared with a conventional distribution
docs.text: Operations on a conventional distribution are imperative (Section 2.5): what was installed and which line of configuration was changed are scattered through the machine's history; moving to a new machine means remembering it all over again. Operations on a declarative system are commits: change the declaration, build, switch, and (if needed) roll back — the workflow of Section 2.2 applies unchanged to an entire operating system.

docs.title: Built-in limitations: learning curve and ecosystem boundaries
docs.text:
A declarative operating system requires you to describe everything in its language — step off its path and you lose its guarantees. Going outside the ecosystem (packaging an obscure piece of software, running a service nobody anticipated) costs more than on a conventional distribution. The engineering judgement: the more controllability a machine demands (servers, infrastructure), the more it is worth it; a highly freewheeling desktop, not necessarily.

Common misconceptions

Thinking "declarative = automation script". A script is a run of commands; when it finishes, it is over, and the machine drifts from then on. Declarative is a standing promise — the system is checked at all times and pulled back to the declared state. The difference is not the degree of automation; it is whether the destination is explicitly declared.

docs.title: Summary and self-check
docs.text:
Three sentences: a declarative operating system writes the state of the whole machine into one declaration; the generation mechanism makes both upgrade and rollback atomic; configuration and packages share a source, and three machines converge on the same state.

Two questions to check yourself:

  1. Why does "rollback cheap and complete" change your courage about upgrading? Explain with the commit philosophy of Section 2.2.
  2. What kind of machine is a poor fit for declarative management? (Hint: who pays the cost of the declaration?)

Maths note. No formulas in this section. One structural fact: the generation model turns system state into an append-only chain, isomorphic to Git's DAG (Section 2.2) — "immutable history + a movable pointer" is a general pattern of reproducibility, recurring from code up to the operating system.

docs.title: Making it legible to others: project structure and technical documentation
The one-line intuition
docs.text: The previous sections made a program runnable and reproducible; this one makes it takeable over by someone else. Both means are astonishingly cheap: directory structure follows conventions, and documentation is classified by the reader's state. Fail at them and the price is that every newcomer (including you, three months later) has to dig through the ruins all over again.

docs.title: The project tree: location is itself documentation
docs.text: src/ holds code, tests/ holds tests, docs/ holds documentation, LICENSE declares the legal identity — none of these conventions is enforced, yet they are the lingua franca of the whole open-source world. Location is itself documentation: nobody has to ask where the tests are, because the convention answers for you. Conversely, a clever structure of your own invention levies a "comprehension tax" on every newcomer.

docs.title: The documentation matrix: classified by the reader's state
docs.text: The commonest documentation failure is piling everything into one giant README. Better organisation slices along two dimensions: the reader's level (beginner/experienced) × the reader's purpose (learning/looking something up/understanding the reasoning), which yields four kinds of documentation each doing its own job — tutorial (walk me through it), how-to guide (solve this specific problem), reference (every parameter, accurate and complete), explanation (why it is designed this way). This matrix is called Diátaxis, and this book's own "one-line intuition / analogy / … / maths note" structure is a variant of it.

docs.title: Writing discipline: write for yourself three months from now
docs.text: The first reader of technical documentation is actually you in the future — the you of three months hence has forgotten the trade-offs you made. So the minimum standard for documentation is not literary grace but that why the decision was made at the time got written down. Combined with the commit discipline of Section 2.2: the commit message records "what changed and why", and the documentation records "how the whole thing works and why it is designed this way".

docs.title: Built-in limitations: documentation rots
docs.text:
Code changed and the documentation did not is more dangerous than no documentation at all — readers will confidently do the wrong thing following the wrong instructions. The only fix is to treat documentation as code: put it in version control, and check in the commit that changes code whether the documentation needs to keep up (this book's lint does exactly that: documentation inconsistent with the structure is blocked). Documentation is not something you finish; it is something you maintain.

Common misconceptions

Thinking "documentation is for people who don't know how to use it". In the Diátaxis matrix, the reference manual is precisely for the strongest users — they remember the usage, not the parameters. Documentation's readers span every level, including the author.

docs.title: Summary and self-check
docs.text:
Three sentences: directory structure follows conventions, and location is itself documentation; documentation is split four ways by the reader's state, each doing its own job; documentation is a maintained artefact, not a delivered one, and it rots unless kept in step.

Two questions to check yourself:

  1. A newcomer cannot find the test files within ten minutes — is the problem in the structure or the documentation?
  2. Why can't a "how-to guide" and a "tutorial" be merged into one piece? (Hint: the readers are in different states — one is learning, one is in a hurry.)

Maths note. No formulas in this section. One organisational fact: the 2×2 of the documentation matrix (level × purpose) shows that the criterion of classification matters more than the classification itself — pick the right slicing dimension and the content of each cell naturally becomes shorter and more precise.

docs.title: The fight over freedom: open source, licences and the currents in developer communities
The one-line intuition
docs.text: A licence is not legal decoration but an enforceable contract: it decides what others may do with your code, and what you must give back. Choosing a licence is essentially choosing a point between "free to use" and "forced to share".

docs.title: Two idealisms: free software and open source
docs.text: In 1983 Stallman started the GNU project, taking the position of free software: software freedom is the user's right — the freedom to run, study, modify and redistribute, none dispensable[47]. In 1998 another group proposed open source: no morality, only effectiveness — the open development model produces better software[48]. The two lists overlap heavily (the OSI's ten criteria for open source and the four freedoms are nearly equivalent); the disagreement is in how the case is argued: one side says "this is a right", the other "this is a method". The argument has never been adjudicated and does not need to be — it lets two sets of values collaborate on the same body of code.

docs.title: The licence spectrum
docs.text:
The two ends of the spectrum: permissive licences (MIT — keep a copyright notice, do as you like with the rest) through to strong copyleft (AGPL — use my code and your whole work must be open-sourced under the same licence). In between are gradations: Apache adds a patent grant; MPL requires only "the file you changed" to be open-sourced; GPL requires the whole derivative work to be open-sourced; AGPL brings "providing a service over the network" into scope too — closing the loophole of the SaaS era.

The mechanism of copyleft is called "infection": code released under the GPL, whichever project it enters, makes that project release under the GPL as well. This is not a punishment but a legal enforcement of the "share" clause — the baton of freedom.

docs.title: The compatibility matrix: check before you choose
docs.text: The practical tool for choosing is the compatibility matrix (Figure 1-63): rows are your project, columns are the code you want to bring in. An MIT project can swallow any code; a GPL project can swallow any code but the whole project must then be GPL; an MIT project that pulls in GPL code is forced to GPL; AGPL code constrains you even if you only call its network service. Pulling in a dependency = signing its licence — the same sentence as "a dependency is borrowed trust" from Section 2.4, seen from the legal side.

docs.title: This book's choice
docs.text: The body text of this book is released under CC BY-SA 4.0 (copyleft: adaptations must credit the author and be shared under the same licence — knowledge should pass hand to hand like GPL code), and the code under Apache-2.0 (permissive: a tool is only valuable when it is used as widely as possible). Copyleft for content, permissive for tools — one licence per kind of asset, a common and self-consistent combination.

docs.title: Built-in limitations: licences protect code, not ideas
docs.text:
A licence constrains the expression of code, not the idea itself — after reading your open-source implementation, someone can rewrite it in another language without violating any licence (ideas are not protected by copyright; what is protected is the specific text you wrote). The AI era adds a new question: is a model trained on open code a "derivative work"? There is no settled answer yet, and it is one more unresolved argument beyond Section 1.6.

Common misconceptions

Two of them. First, "open source = free of charge" — the open-source definition is about freedom, not price; selling open-source software for money is entirely legal. Second, "no licence = use it however you like" — the default is all rights reserved, and with code that has no licence there is legally nothing you may do with it.

docs.title: Summary and self-check
docs.text:
Three sentences: a licence is an enforceable contract, and the spectrum runs from permissive to strong copyleft; copyleft uses an infectious clause to make "sharing" legally mandatory; pulling in a dependency means signing its licence, so check the compatibility matrix before you choose.

Two questions to check yourself:

  1. You want to ship a closed-source product that includes a GPL library — what compliant routes are there?
  2. Why is this book's "copyleft for content, permissive for tools" self-consistent? (Hint: the two assets are used in different ways.)

Maths note. No formulas in this section. One fact about legal structure: the licence chain is a transitive closure — if A (GPL) depends on B (MIT), the combined result only has to satisfy the stronger of the two requirements; when several licences coexist, the strictest one constrains the whole chain.
